E0001.name: extended reality
E0001.text: extended reality; also called: XR. Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR). The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies. Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

E0002.name: virtual reality
E0002.text: virtual reality; also called: VR. Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment. Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment. A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist. The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences. In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

E0003.name: augmented reality
E0003.text: augmented reality; also called: AR. Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content. Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content. Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains. In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.

E0004.name: mixed reality
E0004.text: mixed reality; also called: MR. Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content. There is no agreement among practitioners and in the literature on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR). The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR). One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR. Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

E0005.name: headset
E0005.text: headset; also called: headsets. To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins. In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion. Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take. Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices are the third category of augmented reality devices, also known as room-scale augmented reality or tabletop augmented reality, and they typically use projectors to display graphical information on physical objects; unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, they overlay digital content on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view of the real world. A defining feature of spatial augmented reality (AR) devices is that their display element is not tied to or held by the user, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, and they can provide more natural and intuitive interfaces than these other device categories.

E0006.name: virtual world
E0006.text: virtual world; also called: immersive virtual world, virtual environment, VR environment. To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins. Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world. A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism. Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement. Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

E0007.name: virtual object
E0007.text: virtual object; also called: virtual objects. To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins. The fundamental principle of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system is that it augments the physical environment by adding virtual objects that seem to coexist in the same space as real objects, so the digitally augmented content appears to coexist with the physical space surrounding the user. When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking. Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for building better hardware and for understanding the effects of an extended reality (XR) system on the user by answering questions such as how far away an object appears in a given virtual world, how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, whether the user's head appears at the proper height in the virtual world for the point of view that should correspond to the user's height, where virtual sound appears to come from, why a user feels nauseated, why one system experience is more tiring than another, and what presence is. A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, which is typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, enables users to see and interact with the physical world around them, and it adds virtual objects to the real world or visually enhances real objects.

E0008.name: immersive technology
E0008.text: immersive technology; also called: immersive technologies. Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR). The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies. An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology. Digital heritage preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve heritage, whether cultural, educational, scientific, ecological, or other, and it involves archiving, digitizing, and using immersive technologies such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR). In digital heritage preservation, immersive technologies can recreate a physical space as a virtual world, such as a virtual tour, and, if properly designed, allow users to interact with entities in the virtual world, making the experience more engaging than accessing information through a computer screen.

E0010.name: reality-virtuality continuum
E0010.text: reality-virtuality continuum. The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real. Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content. Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content. One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

E0011.name: augmented virtuality
E0011.text: augmented virtuality. Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment. In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

E0012.name: market size
E0012.text: market size. A market study reports that the extended reality market size was about 20.5 billion US dollars in 2021 and is expected to be about 860 billion US dollars by 2030, an exponential increase. The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent.

E0013.name: hardware
E0013.text: hardware. The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent. The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software. The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content. In virtual reality (VR), an external factor in cybersickness (CS) is a factor that is not subjective to a user's mental or physical condition, and hardware is one category of external factors. Cybersickness (CS) in virtual reality (VR) is not simply a problem of inferior hardware quality; although early users associated it with inferior hardware, many problems persist with advanced technology, so some aspects of devices themselves induce cybersickness.

The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software. A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world. The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware requires proper interaction design and modeling for the user's interaction with input devices, perceptual design and modeling so that stimuli generated by output devices suitably stimulate the user's sense organs, and software to process input data and generate output data. The software part of the virtual reality (VR) data-flow diagram is represented by two components: the virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

E0015.name: metaverse
E0015.text: metaverse. The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field. The metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology, while one broad view is that it reimagines the way humans interact with the digital world. In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction with digital content, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions with occasional three-dimensional interaction. The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software.

E0040.name: head-mounted display
E0040.text: head-mounted display; also called: headset, HMDs, HMD, headsets, VR headset, head-mounted displays. The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s. In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors. In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear. In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs). In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

E0042.name: immersion
E0042.text: immersion; also called: level of immersion. Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world. From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive. Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals. Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world. A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

E0044.text: virtual tour; also called: exploration, immersive virtual tours, virtual tour of the island, virtual tour experience, virtual tours, virtual reality tour, VR tour. Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information. The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually. Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

E0056.name: virtual reality system
E0056.text: virtual reality system; also called: VR system, system. A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects. The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment. An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time. The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system. The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

E0057.name: non-immersive virtual reality system
E0057.text: non-immersive virtual reality system; also called: non-immersive virtual reality application, non-immersive VR systems. From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive. A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user. A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world. Non-immersive virtual reality (VR) includes specifically gaming applications, such as games on PlayStation, Xbox, or similar systems and games like World of Warcraft or similar games, that rely on computer or video game console displays and input devices such as keyboards, mice, and handheld controllers. Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

E0058.name: semi-immersive virtual reality system
E0058.text: semi-immersive virtual reality system. From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive. Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals. Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) can be a three-dimensional virtual environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, a VR box, or a VR headset, with a VR headset being the common example; users typically have no real physical movements, and examples include virtual tours using only a headset, which can be device-based or web-based. Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world. Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

E0059.name: fully immersive virtual reality system
E0059.text: fully immersive virtual reality system. From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive. A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism. Fully immersive virtual reality (VR) systems, such as dedicated virtual shooting game zones, use many devices such as helmets, gloves, body connectors with sense detectors, and body suits, so users view the virtual environment through a helmet or head-mounted display and their actual movements, such as running, jumping, crouching, shooting, and throwing, their reactions, and even a blink of an eye are detected and translated into actions in the virtual world while the user cannot sense anything in the real world. AccuVein is a handheld device with augmented reality (AR) applications that scans a patient's vein network, can indicate the patient's condition, can lead to a 45% reduction in escalation, and, by being pointed at the skin surface, allows the internal vein network to be visualized so the treatment course can be decided. Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) have broadly similar application domains, but VR applications are characterized as immersive, whereas AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than immersive applications. Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones. The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

E0106.name: marker-based augmented reality application
E0106.text: marker-based augmented reality application. Augmented reality (AR) applications are categorized by technology rather than by psychological or immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based augmented reality applications and markerless augmented reality applications. Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view. Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers. Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications are easier to build but difficult to maintain because markers are prone to damage, and a damaged marker may make the application not work. Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

E0107.name: markerless augmented reality application
E0107.text: markerless augmented reality application. Augmented reality (AR) applications are categorized by technology rather than by psychological or immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based augmented reality applications and markerless augmented reality applications. Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications can have four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based. Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects. Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location. Superimposition-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications recognize one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimpose digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.

In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems. E0117.text: computer vision technique; also called: computer-vision techniques, computer vision techniques, computer-vision technique, computer-vision. Implementing a spatial augmented reality (AR) system requires understanding the geometry and lighting conditions of the physical environment for seamless mixing, which can be achieved using advanced depth sensors or computer vision techniques typically included in the system. A virtual world can also be a recorded physical world, made realistic by capturing the real world with cameras and using computer-vision and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) techniques, so virtual reality (VR) software may require support for SLAM or computer-vision techniques.

E0119.name: global positioning system
E0119.text: global positioning system; also called: GPS. Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS). The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments. The global positioning system (GPS) generally offers low accuracy, particularly in indoor environments, and allows only positional tracking. Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system. The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.

Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) have broadly similar application domains, but VR applications are characterized as immersive, whereas AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than immersive applications. Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people. Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering. From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions. A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed.

E0139.name: virtual
E0139.text: virtual. The term virtual means, according to Webster's New Universal Dictionary, being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be attributed to any factual things.

E0140.name: reality
E0140.text: reality. The term reality is defined in dictionary terms as the state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a real or actual thing as distinguished from something merely apparent.

E0141.name: artificial environment
E0141.text: artificial environment; also called: synthetic environment, virtual environment. A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects. The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment. An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time. The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system. The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

A single interface sketch is primarily used to represent a horizontal prototype and is not sufficient to prototype interactions because it does not show the sequence of user actions and the corresponding interface changes needed to execute a task. In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

E0145.text: real time. The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D. The cloud-based video-loading optimization for the Oculus Quest 2 application relied on a cloud server, so it required high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time; if these network connectivity issues were not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.

E0146.text: user interaction; also called: interaction with users. E0147.name: interaction
E0147.text: interaction; also called: real-time interaction, forms of interaction, interaction support, interaction techniques. Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user. Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture. For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings. In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

E0148.name: computer-aided design system
E0148.text: computer-aided design system; also called: CAD system. A computer-aided design (CAD) system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it supports a virtual environment and interaction, it does not support an immersive experience, since the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

E0149.name: video conferencing system
E0149.text: video conferencing system. A video conferencing system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it is interactive, it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience, since it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen and the user remains in the real world, with the screen only aiding interaction.

E0150.name: three-dimensional movie experience
E0150.text: three-dimensional movie experience; also called: 3D movie experience. A three-dimensional (3D) movie experience is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it is not interactive, as the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.

E0151.name: augmented reality system
E0151.text: augmented reality system; also called: AR system, augmented reality systems. The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D. An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times. A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.

E0152.name: three-dimensional
E0152.text: three-dimensional; also called: 3D. The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D. An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times. Sensorama was publicized as having 3D, wide vision, motion, color, stereo sound, smell, wind, and vibrations (haptics), and it stimulated all sensory organs by letting a user feel pre-recorded vibrations, sounds, smells, and wind. Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone. The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

E0153.name: sensory organ
E0153.text: sensory organ; also called: sensory organs. For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ. In the human body, the sensory organs are the hardware of sensing.

E0154.name: physical environment
E0154.text: physical environment; also called: real environment. The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR). One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR. Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

E0155.name: early era
E0155.text: early era. The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases: the early era, which existed before the advent of digital computers, the formative years from roughly 1950 to 1990, the modern phase from 1991 to 2015, and the current growth phase from roughly 2016 onwards. The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

E0158.name: modern phase
E0158.text: modern phase. The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases: the early era, which existed before the advent of digital computers, the formative years from roughly 1950 to 1990, the modern phase from 1991 to 2015, and the current growth phase from roughly 2016 onwards. The modern phase of virtual reality (VR) is the period roughly from 1990 to 2015, about 25 years. The availability of inexpensive headsets, such as the Oculus Rift, greatly spurred interest in virtual reality (VR) towards the end of its modern phase.

E0159.name: current growth phase
E0159.text: current growth phase. E0160.name: historical evolution
E0160.text: historical evolution. The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences. The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

E0161.name: Sir Charles Wheatstone
E0161.text: Sir Charles Wheatstone. Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience. David Brewster's 1860 compact-sized stereoscope was an early form of stereoscopic display that created the illusion of depth in viewed images and, as an advancement over Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device, is roughly considered another step toward practical immersive experiences.

E0163.name: two-dimensional image
E0163.text: two-dimensional image; also called: 2D image, 2D images, 2D regular images. Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience. In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion. Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye. When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects. The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements.

E0164.name: three-dimensional object
E0164.text: three-dimensional object; also called: 3D object. Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience. In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position. In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect. When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

E0165.name: display device
E0165.text: display device; also called: display devices. In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion. Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version. Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering. A display device uses a pixel grid to render an image, and points on that pixel grid can only have integer coordinates.

E0167.name: three-dimensional space
E0167.text: three-dimensional space; also called: 3D space. In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion. Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers. Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air. In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view. In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

E0174.name: sensor
E0174.text: sensor; also called: input device, sensors, tracker, human bodily sensors. Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices). In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements. Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers. The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses.

E0175.name: formative years of virtual reality

E0176.name: computer display
E0176.text: computer display; also called: computer screen, screen. In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors. The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them. In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen. The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view. In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts. Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking. In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

E0201.name: field of view
E0201.text: field of view; also called: FOV, visual field of view. Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision. A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion. Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS). An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience. Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.

E0202.name: data glove
E0202.text: data glove; also called: data gloves. In 1987, two papers appeared in Scientific American, one on the data glove, an input device, and these papers helped shape and popularize the field of virtual reality. Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular. Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction. Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

E0221.name: virtual reality growth phase
E0221.text: virtual reality growth phase; also called: growth phase. In the evolution of virtual reality (VR), the growth phase is the last and continuing phase and began roughly in 2016, when many well-known companies released commercial virtual reality (VR) headsets that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurred growth in the field. The virtual reality (VR) growth phase is a continuing phase because more developments, including better headsets, better immersive displays, and better input devices, will happen, will continue, and may accelerate because there is going to be huge demand.

E0222.name: virtual reality headset
E0222.text: virtual reality headset; also called: headsets, VR headset, VR headsets, VR. In virtual reality (VR) headsets, light emitted from the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye, a combined system that helps the user perceive immersive visual content. Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception. A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over. For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

E0235.name: experimental phase
E0235.text: experimental phase. The historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality: the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present. The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

E0239.name: tracking
E0239.text: tracking; also called: pose estimation and updating, sensing, tracking process, sensor tracking, tracking estimation. In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism. Tracking is an integral hardware component of an extended reality (XR) system. Keeping track of motion in the physical world is a crucial part of any extended reality (XR) system, more importantly in virtual reality (VR) systems. In virtual reality (VR), tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion in the virtual world. In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view.

E0240.name: interaction technique
E0240.text: interaction technique; also called: techniques. The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing. For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques. Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques to be used to interact with the virtual augmentation of the real world because the user's senses are not blocked. Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience.

E0241.name: usability
E0241.text: usability. Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user. The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios. The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

E0245.name: Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype
E0245.text: Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype. Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality (AR) prototype in 1968. The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

E0246.name: cathode ray tube
E0246.text: cathode ray tube; also called: CRT, cathode-ray tube. The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker. The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

E0247.name: optical see-through head-mounted display
E0247.text: optical see-through head-mounted display; also called: optical see-through, optical see-through HMD. Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through. Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

Viewpoint tracking was one of the most significant challenges of augmented reality (AR), and it was addressed so that three-dimensional registration of content could happen accurately. Three-dimensional (3D) registration in augmented reality (AR) means anchoring virtual content in the real world at a suitable place so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects. To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications. ARToolKit is one of the most widely adopted software libraries for developing augmented reality (AR) applications; it is written in C and supports platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS. ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques. ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library: it provides functions that enable a developer to perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.

E0309.name: software development kit
E0309.text: software development kit; also called: SDK, basic software development kit, SDKs, SDK package. In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them. To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts. A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK). When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required. Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.

E0317.name: algorithm
E0317.text: algorithm. The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G. The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G. After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances. The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph. Because the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver's optimal path p_opt may contain hypothetical edges that are not in the original graph G, the algorithm post-processes p_opt into p_dash_opt by checking each path edge and replacing each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G with the shortest path between those endpoints in G.

E0319.name: registration
E0319.text: registration. The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked. Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0. A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction. Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.

E0320.name: sensory stimuli
E0320.text: sensory stimuli. The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs. There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

E0321.name: technological issue
E0321.text: technological issue. There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users. The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.

E0323.name: human factors
E0323.text: human factors; also called: human-factor issue, human factors in system design. Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

E0324.name: presence
E0324.text: presence; also called: sense of presence, user presence, presence measure, user presence ratings, presence ratings, presence results, present. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience. Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer. Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account. Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

E0325.name: extensive
E0325.text: extensive. In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing. Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

E0326.name: sensory modality
E0326.text: sensory modality. Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is. Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

E0327.name: matching
E0327.text: matching. In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing. Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

E0328.name: surrounding
E0328.text: surrounding. Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.
