E0331.name: lighting
E0331.text: lighting; also called: illumination, realistic lighting. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion. The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

E0332.name: frame rate
E0332.text: frame rate; also called: frame rates, frames per second, fps. Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid. To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter. For motion perception in an immersive environment, temporal resolution in a virtual reality (VR) headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second (fps) or 60 fps, with higher frame rates preferred. Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.

E0337.name: perfect presence
E0337.text: perfect presence. Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

E0338.name: uncanny valley effect
E0338.text: uncanny valley effect; also called: uncanny valley, uncanny valley region. The uncanny valley effect is a finding from a scientific study of human perception of artificial objects, originally robots and extendable to digital representations, that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first. In the plot illustrating the uncanny valley effect, with human likeness on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and familiarity on the vertical axis (y-axis), as an artificial object or digital object in virtual reality (VR) becomes more human-like, familiarity first increases for both moving and stationary objects, then decreases, more sharply for moving objects, reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region, typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness, and then increases again. When creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the uncanny valley effect means that trying to match reality exactly with human-like figures or realistic objects may not produce a good experience if their human-likeness falls in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include. The uncanny valley effect in virtual reality (VR) is the phenomenon in which making environments as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience can cause uneasiness or creepiness in the user's mind. To avoid the uncanny valley effect while building virtual reality (VR) systems, one should be aware of representational fidelity, experiential fidelity, and interaction fidelity.

E0339.name: human perception
E0339.text: human perception. Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory. An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

E0343.name: photorealism
E0343.text: photorealism; also called: photorealistic. In virtual reality (VR), presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects; other cues may be equally useful for achieving higher presence. The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience.

E0344.name: representational fidelity
E0344.text: representational fidelity. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence. Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual reality (VR) experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth. The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should be aware of the uncanny valley effect and maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience.

E0345.name: interaction fidelity
E0345.text: interaction fidelity. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence. Interaction fidelity is the degree to which the physical actions for a virtual task correspond to the physical actions for an equivalent real-world task, and it exploits real-world experience. High interaction fidelity involves intense realistic physical actions for virtual tasks, in which real-world physical activities are translated into virtual activities, while very low interaction fidelity involves no physical motion, such as sitting while moving forward in the virtual world by button press. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should be aware of the uncanny valley effect and maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience.

E0346.name: experiential fidelity
E0346.text: experiential fidelity. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence. Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the virtual reality (VR) creator. Low experiential fidelity occurs when a free roaming virtual world with endless possibilities leads every usage to a different experience, because that is not what happens in the real world, while higher experiential fidelity results when real-world constraints are placed on virtual navigation, movement, and interaction, making the virtual experience closer to the real world. A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should be aware of the uncanny valley effect and maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience.

E0347.name: 360-degree video
E0347.text: 360-degree video. The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience. The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements. After processing a larger captured collection and keeping the minimum required material, the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island contains about 600 360-degree images, about 25 360-degree images per location, 5 360-degree videos, 11 two-dimensional (2D) regular videos capturing intangible cultural aspects, and 8 drone videos. In the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island, the high-definition 360-degree image resolution is 6720 by 3360, the drone 360-degree video resolution is 1920 by 960, and the drone video used for cultural and ecological preservation has resolution 3842 by 1920. The average file size in the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is 6.3 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree image, 100 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree video, 34 megabytes (MB) for a two-dimensional (2D) video used to capture cultural and intangible aspects, and 36 megabytes (MB) for a drone video.

E0348.name: display technology
E0348.text: display technology. Combining real and virtual content in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on the device, and the same display issue also exists in virtual reality (VR). The major issues in augmented reality (AR) are mostly technological and consist of proper display technology, proper input mechanisms and technology, and pose estimation and updating, which is popularly called tracking, at the beginning and during system use. In virtual reality (VR), eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.

E0349.name: input modality
E0349.text: input modality; also called: input modalities. Real-time interaction in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable forms of interaction, including different input devices and input modalities, so that the user can interact with digital content overlaid on a representation of the real world.

E0350.name: pose
E0350.text: pose; also called: poses. To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible. Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras. The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors. In outside looking in infrared tracking, cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object detect targets attached to the object and use them to determine the object's pose and position. In inside looking out infrared tracking, the camera is mounted with the user and detects external targets, from which it estimates poses.

E0352.name: orientation
E0352.text: orientation. To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible. In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view. Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

E0353.name: anchor
E0353.text: anchor. Conceptually, pose determination in augmented reality (AR) has two parts, the registration phase and the tracking phase, which can be performed in one phase or as separate phases; the registration phase determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system, and the tracking phase updates that pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move in an AR application, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed. E0358.name: cybersickness
E0358.text: cybersickness; also called: CS, visually induced motion sickness, VIMS, cyber sickness. Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality. A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen. Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor. Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people. Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

The scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) were nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness. The cyber sickness evaluation of the Majuli virtual tour used the SSQ questionnaire and collected pre-exposure and post-exposure data for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor effects, and total severity. The box plots of average pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour system did not generally induce cyber sickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference.

E0371.text: user experience; also called: immersive user experience. Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people. Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience. Each extended reality (XR) engine has its own minimum random access memory (RAM) requirement, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable in a virtual reality (VR) system's hardware for a good user experience. The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

E0372.name: internal factors
E0372.text: internal factors; also called: internal factor. The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content. Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition. The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

E0377.name: motion sickness
E0377.text: motion sickness; also called: MS. Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition. Motion sickness (MS) occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, causing symptoms like nausea and dizziness that are similar to cyber sickness. Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility. Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness (MS) susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, so individuals with higher MS susceptibility are likely to experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms. Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

E0395.name: multiple sclerosis
E0395.text: multiple sclerosis. Individuals with neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

E0396.name: standing posture
E0396.text: standing posture. A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

E0397.name: anxiety
E0397.text: anxiety. Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

E0402.name: display resolution
E0402.text: display resolution; also called: resolution. Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K. Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast. In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the system was developed for the Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display (HMD), with a display resolution of 1920 by 1832 pixels per eye, and the HMD was connected to a personal computer (PC) via an enabled Oculus Link, the standard setup. The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

E0403.name: latency
E0403.text: latency; also called: minimal latency. Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world. In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR), cybersickness (CS) increases with latency; the more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce cybersickness. Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

E0404.name: latency jitter
E0404.text: latency jitter. Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time. Latency jitter causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery and can lead to inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness (CS).

E0405.name: display type
E0405.text: display type. Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS. The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.

E0413.name: input method
E0413.text: input method. In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).

E0414.name: hand controller
E0414.text: hand controller; also called: hand controllers. In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS). In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

E0415.name: treadmill
E0415.text: treadmill; also called: treadmills. Treadmills are output devices that provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs. Omnidirectional treadmills are common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

E0416.name: motion sensor
E0416.text: motion sensor; also called: motion sensors. In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS). Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

E0417.name: motion controller
E0417.text: motion controller; also called: motion controllers. In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

E0418.name: joystick
E0418.text: joystick; also called: joysticks. In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller. World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area. Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR. The system design implemented a controlled navigation technique to minimize cybersickness, in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort and reduces the chances of discomfort. In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

E0419.text: gamepad controller. In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

E0422.name: content factor
E0422.text: content factor. The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.

E0423.name: visual motion
E0423.text: visual motion. The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity. Visual motion, the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality (VR) environment, is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness (CS), and higher visual motion can increase the risk of cyber sickness while the way the content moves also affects cyber sickness and its severity. Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS). Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cyber sickness (CS), but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cyber sickness.

E0424.name: means of locomotion
E0424.text: means of locomotion; also called: locomotion. Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness. Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence. The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

E0425.name: type of content
E0425.text: type of content. The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity. The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content. The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

E0426.name: duration
E0426.text: duration. The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity. The average duration in the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is 4 minutes for a 360-degree video, about 40 seconds for a two-dimensional (2D) cultural video that captures intangible aspects, and 30 seconds for a drone video. The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

E0427.name: visual complexity
E0427.text: visual complexity. Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

E0428.name: vection
E0428.text: vection. Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS). Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

E0429.name: self-motion
E0429.text: self-motion. Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

E0431.name: visual motion stimulus

E0432.name: height
E0432.text: height; also called: h. The severity of cyber sickness (CS) also significantly increases with larger height and faster speed in a virtual environment. In the empirical study, participant heights were recorded because earlier studies indicate that height affects walking behavior, and the participants' heights ranged from 150 to 184 centimeters. In the natural walking-speed model, f is the instantaneous step frequency and h is the height of the user. V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

E0433.name: speed
E0433.text: speed. Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

E0434.name: viewpoint
E0434.text: viewpoint; also called: camera position. The viewpoint during motion is also an important factor for cyber sickness (CS). In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation. For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized. The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.

E0435.name: turbulent visual motion
E0435.text: turbulent visual motion. Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cyber sickness (CS), but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cyber sickness.

E0436.name: angular velocity
E0436.text: angular velocity. Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis. A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence. In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes. Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures. In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

E0437.name: rotation
E0437.text: rotation; also called: rotation values. The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

E0438.name: x axis
E0438.text: x axis. Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis. In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

E0439.name: y axis
E0439.text: y axis. Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis. In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

E0440.name: z axis
E0440.text: z axis. Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis. In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

E0441.name: sensory mismatch
E0441.text: sensory mismatch; also called: mismatch, sensory conflict. Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness. In an immersive virtual reality (VR) system, interfering with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing can create a mismatch because the brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time. A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea. A mismatch between the brain's sensory inputs and its familiar processing can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware of the conflict and immediately understand that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real. Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

E0442.name: control over motion
E0442.text: control over motion; also called: control mechanism, motion control. Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence. The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

E0443.name: hand-based motion control
E0443.text: hand-based motion control. The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

E0444.name: whole-body motion control
E0444.text: whole-body motion control. The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

E0445.name: transition type
E0445.text: transition type; also called: type of transition. The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

E0446.name: teleportation
E0446.text: teleportation; also called: target-based teleportation, teleport, teleportation-type movement. The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping. Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement. Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems. Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation. Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

E0447.name: naturalistic free movement
E0447.text: naturalistic free movement. The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

E0448.name: field of vision
E0448.text: field of vision. Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision. A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses superimpose digital images or information onto the wearer's field of vision directly on the lens.

E0449.name: head movement
E0449.text: head movement; also called: head motion. An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience. Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement. Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

E0450.name: action content
E0450.text: action content. The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content. For users with a high preference for adrenaline sports or adventurous things, exposure to action content, fast movements, or abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment may not lead to severe cybersickness (CS) compared with users who are not exposed to such sports or adventures, because they are already accustomed to such behavior and environments.

E0454.text: static content. The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

E0455.name: genre
E0455.text: genre. The genre of a virtual environment affects cybersickness (CS), and content based on horror scenes is likely to induce more CS than pleasant general content.

E0456.name: geometry
E0456.text: geometry. The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides. In Unity's mesh rendering workflow, the mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

E0457.name: terrain
E0457.text: terrain. The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides. The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

E0458.name: weather conditions
E0458.text: weather conditions. Weather conditions in a virtual environment affect the induction of cybersickness (CS); stormy conditions are more likely to cause higher CS than clear weather conditions.

E0459.name: exposure duration
E0459.text: exposure duration; also called: exposure time, duration of exposure, VR session duration. Virtual reality (VR) exposure duration is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and prolonged exposure through head-mounted displays (HMDs) leads to greater cybersickness. Cybersickness (CS) increases with virtual reality (VR) exposure time when users use different locomotion controllers during navigation tasks in a virtual environment, and the effect of the locomotion technique used to move from one point to another on cybersickness is further complicated by longer duration. Continuous exposure to live-action 180-degree videos results in higher cybersickness (CS), and the increase in cybersickness grows with exposure time. The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world. In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

Hybrid models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation can combine the strengths of transparent and black-box models by providing good predictive accuracy and some interpretability, making them useful in application domains where both high accuracy and transparency are essential, such as medical diagnosis.

E0553.name: cybersickness mitigation
E0553.text: cybersickness mitigation; also called: CS mitigation. Because complete prevention of cybersickness (CS) is generally not possible, cybersickness mitigation uses measures to reduce or eliminate cybersickness or at least lessen its impact. Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience. Cybersickness (CS) mitigation is considered from two important perspectives, the developer's perspective and the user's perspective, because even a good developer solution may fail to prevent cybersickness if the user does not use the system properly or as expected.

E0556.name: field of view adjustment
E0556.text: field of view adjustment; also called: FOV adjustment. Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications. Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow. Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts. A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience. A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

E0557.name: dynamic visual blur
E0557.text: dynamic visual blur. Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications. Dynamic visual blur is a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness (CS) in which blurring means obscuring or reducing clarity, and it has two types: depth-of-field blur, which uses well-known depth cues in human vision, and peripheral blur, also called dynamic non-salient region blurring.

E0558.name: rest frame
E0558.text: rest frame; also called: rest frames. Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds, with examples including clouds, grids, and a virtual nose.

E0559.name: optical-flow manipulation

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

E0560.name: hardware-level alteration

Hardware-level alterations can reduce or eliminate cybersickness (CS) by modifying existing hardware to different degrees or by proposing completely new hardware. Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a sparse peripheral display that expands a head-mounted display (HMD) periphery with a colorful LED matrix, and miniature LED screens placed in the HMD. Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a Noble camera setup twin cam that reduces motion blur and cybersickness, and a hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig that can be used to reduce cybersickness. Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps using additional hardware, and it was found to reduce cybersickness (CS) to a great extent.

E0602.name: virtual reality session
E0602.text: virtual reality session. To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

E0603.name: exposure
E0603.text: exposure. To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky. Users can attempt habituation to a virtual environment through a two-stage approach in which users first use repeated short-duration exposures until undesirable symptoms appear, then use repeated longer-duration exposures after full recovery from cybersickness (CS) symptoms. In the virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation, participants completed the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) before exploration as a pre-exposure assessment, meaning before exposure to the system, completed the SSQ again after the experimental session as a post-exposure cybersickness measure, and completed the presence questionnaire (QEP) after exploration. The 45 to 50 minute exploration time was estimated from pilot studies, trials, and literature to give users sufficient time to explore the large island and obtain heritage information while minimizing the possibility of cybersickness, which depends on exposure.

In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism. In a complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, the organism component, which typically refers to the human user, is equally important to account for as the VR hardware component and cannot be omitted because the user is always present.

E0612.name: virtual reality hardware
E0612.text: virtual reality hardware; also called: VR hardware, hardware. The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment. Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience. Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior. Virtual reality (VR) hardware is not limited to only the computer, head-mounted display (HMD), or controller used by the user; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment. Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

E0614.name: data flow
E0614.text: data flow; also called: bidirectional data flow, data-flow diagram. In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism. In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions. In a virtual reality (VR) system, bidirectional data flows occur between the virtual reality hardware, the surrounding physical world, and the user (organism), with tracking and stimulation occurring between the user and the virtual reality hardware. The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware works by the user operating input devices to generate data that is sent to and processed by the virtual reality system, and by sending the processed data back to output devices that generate stimuli to suitably affect the user's sense organs. The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware requires proper interaction design and modeling for the user's interaction with input devices, perceptual design and modeling so that stimuli generated by output devices suitably stimulate the user's sense organs, and software to process input data and generate output data.

The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses. The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

E0619.text: button press; also called: button presses. In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

E0621.name: eye movement
E0621.text: eye movement; also called: eye movements. In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts. Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take. Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, and the device is equipped with detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures. In virtual reality (VR), eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking. In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

E0623.name: surrounding physical environment
E0623.text: surrounding physical environment; also called: environment. The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment. The surrounding physical environment is considered part of the virtual reality (VR) system because the user may respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, and may not be completely detached from the real world, so the environment may affect the user's behavior while interacting with the virtual world. A user's physical movement while interacting with the virtual world may change the surrounding physical environment. Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience. Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

E0624.name: tracker
E0624.text: tracker; also called: trackers. Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience. Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking. In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. Eye-tracking systems can be part of other trackers and can be head-mounted or remotely attached to a display or an external display.

E0627.name: controller
E0627.text: controller; also called: handheld input device. Virtual reality (VR) hardware is not limited to only the computer, head-mounted display (HMD), or controller used by the user; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment. Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller. Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

E0628.name: visual display
E0628.text: visual display. Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose. Visual displays are displays meant to stimulate the visual sense, that is the eyes. The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.

E0629.name: tracking device
E0629.text: tracking device. In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.

E0630.name: virtual reality input device
E0630.text: virtual reality input device; also called: VR input devices, input devices. Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

E0631.name: hand input device
E0631.text: hand input device; also called: hand input devices. Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers. Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR. Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

E0632.name: non-hand input device
E0632.text: non-hand input device; also called: non-hand input devices. Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

E0633.name: world-grounded device
E0633.text: world-grounded device; also called: world-grounded hand input device, world-grounded hand input devices, world-grounded devices. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area.

E0634.name: non-tracked handheld controller
E0634.text: non-tracked handheld controller; also called: non-tracked handheld controllers. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers. Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence because the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the position of the virtual hands in the virtual world, creating discomfort about whether the user is performing the task appropriately and affecting the perception of presence in the virtual world.

E0635.name: tracked handheld controller
E0635.text: tracked handheld controller; also called: tracked handheld controllers. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

E0636.name: hand-worn device
E0636.text: hand-worn device; also called: hand-worn hand input device, hand-worn hand input devices, hand-worn devices. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular. The advantages of hand-worn hand input devices are natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction, comfortable hand positions, no line-of-sight issue unlike some controller-based input, and the ability of the user's hands and fingers to fully interact with real objects, making different sorts of perception possible. Issues with hand-worn hand input devices are that recognizing many gestures requires users to recalibrate often or to learn and remember many gestures, which can create problems for different user categories, and that long exposure time can become uncomfortable because the hands may become sweaty.

E0637.name: bare-hand input
E0637.text: bare-hand input; also called: bare-hand inputs. Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs. Bare-hand inputs are the most natural hand input interactions: the system tracks the user's bare hand using computer vision techniques, the user does not need to wear anything or use any external device, and computer vision algorithms detect the user's gestures and translate them into commands in the virtual environment, leaving the user's hands completely free. The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

E0670.name: non-hand-based input devices

Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view. E0671.name: gaze

E0681.name: input
E0681.text: input. The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor. Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability. Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

E0682.name: output
E0682.text: output. The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor. Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

E0683.name: processor
E0683.text: processor. The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor. In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default. Modern central processing unit (CPU) processors are quite powerful, but they have many other tasks to do, so a CPU-only virtual reality (VR) processing system with minimal graphics processing unit (GPU) support can have performance issues, and GPU support is preferable. The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application. The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, and does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer.

E0684.name: non-hand input technique
E0684.text: non-hand input technique; also called: non-hand input techniques, non-hand input method. Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking. Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality (VR) that tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes. Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

E0685.name: full-body tracking
E0685.text: full-body tracking. Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking. Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality (VR) that tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes. Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves. There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking. In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.

E0690.name: camera-based tracking
E0690.text: camera-based tracking; also called: camera-based full-body tracking. There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking. In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

E0693.name: inertial measurement unit
E0693.text: inertial measurement unit; also called: IMU. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs). In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes. Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

E0694.name: camera
E0694.text: camera; also called: cameras. In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems. Augmented reality (AR) headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors, and some of these sensors may or may not also be present in virtual reality (VR) headsets. The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities. Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset. Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

Commercial sensors capable of detecting 3D structure information from the environment became affordable in recent years, a trend that started with the introduction of the Microsoft Kinect device, and similar devices are available. Kinect Fusion, an augmented reality (AR) system by Microsoft and an example of 3D structure tracking, uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments, and the models are also used for tracking the pose of the Kinect.
