The hidden wizard in the 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup heard the user's speech through the microphone that was also connected to a computer speaker, typed the corresponding characters, and the characters were transmitted to the user's screen, making the user believe that the speech had been automatically converted, although no automatic technology existed at that time to convert the speech into the displayed text.

E0703.name: processing element
E0703.text: processing element; also called: processing part, computer. In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices. The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion. The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).

E0704.text: input sensor. E0705.name: output device
E0705.text: output device; also called: hardware output devices, output devices. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them. In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the system was developed for the Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display (HMD), with a display resolution of 1920 by 1832 pixels per eye, and the HMD was connected to a personal computer (PC) via an enabled Oculus Link, the standard setup. In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the stimuli were rendered on a 64-bit computer running Windows 11 Professional operating system (OS), equipped with a 3.6 GHz quad-core processor and a 4GB GeForce GTX 1080 graphics processing unit (GPU). Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

E0708.name: graphics processing unit
E0708.text: graphics processing unit; also called: GPU. A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU). A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process. In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory. An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering. A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

Each extended reality (XR) engine has its own minimum random access memory (RAM) requirement, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable in a virtual reality (VR) system's hardware for a good user experience.

E0713.name: rendering
E0713.text: rendering; also called: rendering process, graphics rendering, rendered, scan conversion. Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware. In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses. From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions. Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses. Among the 27 participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, 21 had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output. The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.

E0720.text: graphics card. Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering. A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features. In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

E0721.name: multicore processor
E0721.text: multicore processor. In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

E0722.name: computational capacity
E0722.text: computational capacity. In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

E0723.name: unicore processor
E0723.text: unicore processor. In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

E0724.name: extended reality engine
E0724.text: extended reality engine; also called: XR engine. An extended reality (XR) engine is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality (VR) experiences. Each extended reality (XR) engine has its own minimum random access memory (RAM) requirement, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable in a virtual reality (VR) system's hardware for a good user experience.

E0725.name: middleware
E0725.text: middleware. Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware. A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed. Using a game engine as middleware can avoid substantial initial effort but may be cumbersome for implementing ideas not part of standard video games, and if the engine is not specifically a virtual reality (VR) engine, the developer loses some flexibility. A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions.

E0726.name: audio output
E0726.text: audio output. Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

E0727.name: motion platform
E0727.text: motion platform; also called: motion platforms, platforms. Motion platforms are hardware output devices that move the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks. Use of motion platforms may result in motion sickness, which can be reduced by decreasing the conflict between visual motion and the perceived motion in the real world. Motion platforms can be active, meaning they are controlled by computer simulation, or passive, meaning they are controlled by the user with no direct computer control, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms.

E0728.name: sensory output system
E0728.text: sensory output system; also called: other sensory outputs. Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose. Other sensory output systems for taste and smell in virtual reality (VR) are premature, not widely used, available, or popular, and are mostly confined to highly specialized environments or research domains.

E0729.name: world-fixed display
E0729.text: world-fixed display. The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary. A world-fixed display renders graphics onto a surface or screen that is fixed and does not move with the user's head; the display is not moving, while the user can move within a physical space. World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave. The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves. A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

E0730.name: regular display
E0730.text: regular display. The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary. Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

E0731.name: monoscopic viewing
E0731.text: monoscopic viewing. A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.

E0732.name: stereoscopic viewing
E0732.text: stereoscopic viewing. A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.

E0733.name: non-see-through head-mounted display
E0733.text: non-see-through head-mounted display; also called: non-see-through, non-see-through HMD. Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through. Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

E0734.name: video see-through head-mounted display
E0734.text: video see-through head-mounted display; also called: video see-through, video see-through HMD. Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

E0739.text: haptic device; also called: haptic devices, computer-controlled haptic device, computer-controlled haptic devices. Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices. Passive haptic devices are static real-world physical objects that match the shape of virtual objects and are not controlled by the computer, whereas active haptic devices are physical objects or physical feedback controlled by the computer that provide a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects. Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin. Self-grounded haptic devices are worn or held by the user and move with the user, with handheld controllers as examples, whereas world-grounded haptic devices are physically attached to the real world, cannot be moved, and can provide the sense of fully solid objects that do not move.

E0740.name: stereo perspective view
E0740.text: stereo perspective view. The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

E0741.name: three-dimensional scene
E0741.text: three-dimensional scene; also called: 3D scene. The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves. Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object. The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane. The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system. In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

E0744.text: tablet; also called: tablets. Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices. Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices are familiar devices such as smartphones or tablets and are the most common and accessible devices used in AR. In augmented reality (AR) hardware, head-mounted displays (HMDs), glasses, handheld devices, and spatial AR systems are bulky or require elaborate setups, and smartphones and tablets can be difficult to hold for a long time.

E0747.text: speaker; also called: speakers, computer speaker. The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities. Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset. The hidden wizard in the 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup heard the user's speech through the microphone that was also connected to a computer speaker, typed the corresponding characters, and the characters were transmitted to the user's screen, making the user believe that the speech had been automatically converted, although no automatic technology existed at that time to convert the speech into the displayed text.

E0751.name: touch perception
E0751.text: touch perception; also called: sense of touch. Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices. When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense. Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception, and it is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects as part of touch perception. Haptic perception can be thought of at different levels: receptors in the skin receive input from the real world and process the information to perceive something through touch, while higher-level perception requires object manipulations that are called haptic explorations. Haptic perception and haptic exploration offer an extra dimension to virtual reality (VR) by letting users feel the virtual environment through the sense of touch, which gives users a better feeling of the virtual world and helps them feel truly immersed in the virtual world, and because immersion in the real world also involves haptic exploration, adding haptic exploration to a virtual world increases the immersive experience.

E0763.text: omnidirectional treadmill; also called: omnidirectional treadmills. E0766.name: augmented reality device
E0766.text: augmented reality device; also called: AR device. Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses. Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices. Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories. Augmented reality (AR) head-up displays are typically found in cars. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

E0767.name: augmented reality headset
E0767.text: augmented reality headset; also called: AR headset, headset, AR headsets. Generally, augmented reality (AR) headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view. Augmented reality (AR) headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors, and some of these sensors may or may not also be present in virtual reality (VR) headsets. The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available. Virtual reality (VR) headsets may not include some advanced features of augmented reality (AR) headsets and typically have fewer components than an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens, because VR does not need to provide a real-world view.

E0768.name: smart glasses
E0768.text: smart glasses; also called: glasses. Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses. Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices. The application domains of augmented reality (AR) device categories include headsets and smart glasses in education, retail, healthcare, tourism, and manufacturing; handheld devices in education, retail, e-commerce, tourism, and real estate; projection-based systems and spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) in industrial design, healthcare, training, retail, gaming, education, art and design, medical training, industrial applications, and entertainment; head-up displays in gaming experiences, medicine, wearables, and sports; and AR contact lenses in medical development. If a system is to be deployed on a specified hardware platform, head-mounted display (HMD), or smart glasses, and that platform provides features or functions not included in the built-in support provided by the Unity environment, the developer imports software development kits (SDKs) or packages to access and use those platform-specific functions.

E0769.name: handheld device
E0769.text: handheld device; also called: handheld devices. Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices. Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices are the third category of augmented reality devices, also known as room-scale augmented reality or tabletop augmented reality, and they typically use projectors to display graphical information on physical objects; unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, they overlay digital content on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view of the real world. A defining feature of spatial augmented reality (AR) devices is that their display element is not tied to or held by the user, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, and they can provide more natural and intuitive interfaces than these other device categories.

E0772.name: head-up display
E0772.text: head-up display; also called: AR head-up display, heads-up display, HUD, HUDs. A head-up display (HUD) is an augmented reality (AR) display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible and only the content is visible, but borders or shades may be visible. Head-up displays (HUDs) are commonly used in cars and aircraft.

E0773.name: augmented reality contact lens
E0773.text: augmented reality contact lens; also called: AR contact lens, AR contact lenses. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are an emerging display category and a future wearable technology; they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, are not visible to outsiders, and are still in the realm of the future. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses superimpose digital images or information onto the wearer's field of vision directly on the lens. E0802.text: gyroscope. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs). In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes. Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.

E0836.name: projection mapping display
E0836.text: projection mapping display; also called: projection mapping displays. Projection mapping displays can be interacted with by rotating, pinching, zooming in, or zooming out.

E0837.name: wearable technology
E0837.text: wearable technology. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are an emerging display category and a future wearable technology; they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, are not visible to outsiders, and are still in the realm of the future.

E0838.name: imager
E0838.text: imager. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

E0839.name: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology
E0839.text: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology; also called: CMOS, CMOS technology. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

E0840.name: wireless component
E0840.text: wireless component. Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

E0841.name: smart contact lens project
E0841.text: smart contact lens project; also called: Google's smart contact lens project. Examples of current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses include Google's smart contact lens project, InnoVega's eye optic system, and Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens.

E0842.name: eye optic system
E0842.text: eye optic system; also called: InnoVega's eye optic system. Examples of current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses include Google's smart contact lens project, InnoVega's eye optic system, and Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens.

E0843.name: sense-organ tracking
names: tracking of the user's sense organs
E0843.text: sense-organ tracking; also called: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking of the user's sense organs. Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user. Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

E0844.name: body-part tracking
names: tracking the user's other body parts
tracking of the user's other body parts
E0844.text: body-part tracking; also called: tracking the user's other body parts, tracking of the user's other body parts. Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user. Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone. For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience. A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

E0845.name: environment tracking
names: tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user
E0845.text: environment tracking; also called: tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user, tracking the surrounding environment. Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user. Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in augmented reality (AR), but also important in virtual reality (VR). In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked. In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

E0846.name: sense organ
E0846.text: sense organ. The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which is the lowest level, to perception, which is at a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

E0847.name: eye
E0847.text: eye; also called: eyes. Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears. The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose). The eyes contain photoreceptors, which are activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light and therefore target only visible light. Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing photopic vision, which is color perception, while light waves outside the visible light spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception.

E0848.name: ear
E0848.text: ear. Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears. The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

E0849.name: body-controlled degree of freedom
E0849.text: body-controlled degree of freedom; also called: body-controlled degrees of freedom. Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

E0850.name: avatar
E0850.text: avatar; also called: avatars. Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone. Wearable electromechanical trackers are worn on a person's body and track and translate the movements of that person into animated avatar movement in a virtual world. A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor. When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required. OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

E0851.name: virtual hand
E0851.text: virtual hand; also called: virtual hands. Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone. A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking. Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea and uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects. In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), the user selects an object using a ray casting technique, and when the ray intersects the desired object, the user's virtual hand moves automatically to the object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object. In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), after the user's virtual hand attaches to the object, the technique switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation.

E0852.name: facial expression
E0852.text: facial expression; also called: facial expressions. Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone. In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

E0853.name: matched zone
E0853.text: matched zone. A matched zone is a place where the real world and the virtual world perfectly align; it corresponds to the safe real-world region where a user's physical movement is restricted, although the virtual world is not similarly confined, and movement within that region is translated to movement in other parts of the virtual world. In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle. Virtual reality (VR) software should include developer support for resolving matched-motion challenges, such as deciding which real-world motions to reflect and creating a correspondence between a user's physical motion in the matched zone and a different virtual motion. User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone.

E0854.name: movement
E0854.text: movement. For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience.

E0855.name: input signal
E0855.text: input signal; also called: explicit input signal. A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

E0856.name: body configuration
E0856.text: body configuration. A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

E0857.name: physical object
E0857.text: physical object; also called: physical objects. Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in augmented reality (AR), but also important in virtual reality (VR). In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space. In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked. In virtual reality (VR), tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience.

E0858.name: real-world view
E0858.text: real-world view. In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space. 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

E0859.name: digital content
E0859.text: digital content. In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

E0860.name: user tracking
E0860.text: user tracking; also called: tracking the user. In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked.

E0861.name: touch feedback
E0861.text: touch feedback. In virtual reality (VR), tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience. To give the feeling of touching a real object surface in a virtual world, using real objects to provide touch feedback is generally considered less challenging than creating a computer-controlled haptic device.

E0862.name: telepresence
E0862.text: telepresence. In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

E0863.name: live capture
E0863.text: live capture. In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

E0864.name: tracking method
E0864.text: tracking method. The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types. Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, and it can be based on any tracking method, so it is not a fundamentally new tracking method. A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, formed by combining basic tracking methods, and emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker.

E0865.name: tracker position
E0865.text: tracker position. The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types. Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking.

E0866.name: tracking process
E0866.text: tracking process. The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

E0867.name: tracker types
E0867.text: tracker types. The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

E0868.name: outside-in tracking
E0868.text: outside-in tracking. Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking. In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. Most virtual reality (VR) headsets today that use external sensors fall under outside-in tracking. Outside-in tracking is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed and works only when the user is in that environment within the sensor range, whereas inside-out tracking has no such restriction because the user wears the sensors or the sensors are attached to the user.

E0869.name: inside-out tracking
E0869.text: inside-out tracking. Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking. Outside-in tracking is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed and works only when the user is in that environment within the sensor range, whereas inside-out tracking has no such restriction because the user wears the sensors or the sensors are attached to the user. Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors required for tracking are located within the device used for the experience, such as the head-mounted display (HMD) in virtual reality (VR), which is more common, so no other external devices are needed. Examples of inside-out tracking are Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, and Qualcomm VR820.

E0870.name: external sensor
E0870.text: external sensor; also called: external tracker. E0871.name: motion
E0871.text: motion. In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation. The auditory, touch, and balance senses involve mechanoreceptors that sense motion, vibration, or gravitational force. In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported. In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold.

E0877.name: calibration
E0877.text: calibration. The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error. In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a. In the calibration stage for inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, the objective is to make the measured angular velocity (omega_g) and the actual angular velocity (omega_a) as close as possible, which means reducing the measurement error to as small a value as possible. One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

E0878.name: integration
E0878.text: integration. The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment. Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

E0879.name: drift correction
E0879.text: drift correction. The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error. Drift correction is usually done with the help of extra sensors and, in general, requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift. For drift correction, a gyroscope may be used together with other sensors such as cameras, and in an inertial measurement unit (IMU), accelerometer and magnetometer readings can be used in addition to gyroscope values. A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

E0880.text: sensor error. In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

E0881.name: sensory measurement

E0882.name: estimation error
E0882.text: estimation error. In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

E0883.name: linear acceleration
E0883.text: linear acceleration. In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

E0884.name: magnetic field strength
E0884.text: magnetic field strength. In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

E0885.name: drift error
E0885.text: drift error. Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

E0886.name: measured angular velocity
E0886.text: measured angular velocity. In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a. In the calibration stage for inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, the objective is to make the measured angular velocity (omega_g) and the actual angular velocity (omega_a) as close as possible, which means reducing the measurement error to as small a value as possible. One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship. The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal. A simple calibration method compares the paired samples by computing, for n pairs, the sum of the squared differences between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a, and it finds the constants C1 and C2 that minimize this sum; this classical optimization is linear least squares regression, one of many techniques that is used here for simplicity.

E0894.name: calibrated value
E0894.text: calibrated value. After the constants C1 and C2 are determined, calibration mathematically transforms the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value omega_cal, defined as omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, mapping the inexpensive measured angular velocity omega_g to the closest possible match with the actual value rather than by using an actually expensive or highly accurate sensor.

E0895.name: initial orientation
E0895.text: initial orientation; also called: initial pose. Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0. A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction. Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

E0896.name: initial alignment
E0896.text: initial alignment. Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0. E0949.name: fiducial tracking
E0949.text: fiducial tracking. Visible light tracking is classified into three tracking techniques: fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking. Fiducial tracking adds fiducials, which are artificial landmarks in the environment, to aid registration and tracking of the object being tracked. The complexity of fiducial tracking depends on the kind of fiducial used, such as small colored light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or pieces of paper, multi-ring fiducials for detection at greater distances, proportional width ring fiducials whose appearance changes with distance, or constant width ring fiducials whose ring width remains constant.

E0950.name: natural feature tracking
E0950.text: natural feature tracking. Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques. In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections. In natural feature tracking, unique descriptors are calculated for each detected feature, and their role is to identify and differentiate one feature from other features. In natural feature tracking, camera pose is estimated by using the calculated feature descriptors to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked. Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

E0969.text: simultaneous localization and mapping; also called: SLAM. A mental model can be created by aiding the user to get, understand, or infer knowledge through the traditional methods of systematic study of a map of a place, exploration of real space, exploration of a copy of the real space or a model of the real space, or any combination of these methods. Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points. When the user reaches the riverbank in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, a tablet interface appears that lets the user select a location on a map and move to that particular location. The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation supports movement from one point to another using an overall island minimap on the tablet interface, in which each white dot represents a 360-degree image and the user's current location is marked in green.

E0971.name: localization
E0971.text: localization; also called: localizing. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking. For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.

E0972.name: robot navigation
E0972.text: robot navigation. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) was originally developed for robot navigation and subsequently adapted for augmented reality.

E0973.name: parallel tracking and mapping
E0973.text: parallel tracking and mapping; also called: PTAM. Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) that allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities. Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) was specifically designed for augmented reality. Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) improved both the accuracy of tracking and the overall performance. Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is more suitable for smaller environments because the computational requirements for larger environments are quite high.

E0974.name: mapping

Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.

E0977.name: computational requirement
E0977.text: computational requirement; also called: computational requirements. Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is more suitable for smaller environments because the computational requirements for larger environments are quite high. Rendering the Majuli application's rich multimodal content, which can be interactively changed and includes videos and animations, involves a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a simple static image and requires fast storage and retrieval support for real-time realistic interactive rendering.

E0978.name: three-dimensional structure tracking
E0978.text: three-dimensional structure tracking; also called: 3D structure tracking, 3D structure sensing. 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view. Kinect Fusion, an augmented reality (AR) system by Microsoft and an example of 3D structure tracking, uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments, and the models are also used for tracking the pose of the Kinect.

E0979.text: commercial sensor; also called: commercial sensors. 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view. The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements. In the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island, three-dimensional (3D) models were created from captured images to recreate the landscape, preserve ecological heritage, and recreate tangible architectural heritage.

E0988.name: inertial tracker
E0988.text: inertial tracker; also called: inertial sensors. Inertial trackers are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration, and they measure only changes rather than absolute values. Inertial trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and are part of the device that the user is using, for example most smartphones and head-mounted displays (HMDs) nowadays, so they have no range limitation and can be readily used for tracking. Hybrid software-level sensors can be designed using the primary inertial sensors (a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer) and can be part of the device. Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

E0989.name: microelectromechanical system
E0989.text: microelectromechanical system; also called: MEMS. Inertial trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and are part of the device that the user is using, for example most smartphones and head-mounted displays (HMDs) nowadays, so they have no range limitation and can be readily used for tracking.

E0990.name: hybrid software-level sensor

E0994.text: light-based sensing. Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

E0995.name: acoustic sensing
E0995.text: acoustic sensing. Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).

E0996.name: positional tracking
E0996.text: positional tracking. The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments. The global positioning system (GPS) generally offers low accuracy, particularly in indoor environments, and allows only positional tracking.

E0997.name: real time kinematic
E0997.text: real time kinematic; also called: RTK. Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system.

E0998.name: hybrid tracking system
E0998.text: hybrid tracking system. The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

E0999.name: motion capture
E0999.text: motion capture. Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, and it can be based on any tracking method, so it is not a fundamentally new tracking method. Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements. Motion capture need not be real-time tracking; it can be non-real-time tracking as well.

E1000.name: wearable suit
E1000.text: wearable suit. Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

E1001.name: facial tracker
E1001.text: facial tracker. Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

E1002.text: full body tracking device. E1004.text: non-real-time tracking. Motion capture need not be real-time tracking; it can be non-real-time tracking as well.

E1005.name: external display
E1005.text: external display. Eye-tracking systems can be part of other trackers and can be head-mounted or remotely attached to a display or an external display.

E1006.name: optical tracking
E1006.text: optical tracking. Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

E1007.name: camera-based tracking device
E1007.text: camera-based tracking device; also called: high-resolution camera-based tracking device. Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

E1008.name: infrared lighting-based eye tracking
E1008.text: infrared lighting-based eye tracking. Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

E1009.name: video-oculography
E1009.text: video-oculography; also called: VOG. Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

E1010.text: gaze point. Eye-tracking systems typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

E1012.name: hybrid tracker
E1012.text: hybrid tracker. A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, formed by combining basic tracking methods, and emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker. Typically, hybrid trackers have been found to perform better than single-technology-based tracking.
