E1015.name: virtual reality software
E1015.text: virtual reality software; also called: VR software, virtual reality software system. The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses. From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions. Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware. In practice, a virtual reality (VR) developer may need to implement much functionality from scratch instead of providing only high-level descriptions that software automatically converts to low-level details.

E1016.name: augmented reality hardware
E1016.text: augmented reality hardware; also called: AR hardware. The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

E1017.name: human sense organs
E1017.text: human sense organs. The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

E1018.name: human senses
E1018.text: human senses; also called: human sense. The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose). Among the six human senses, balance is a sense for which there is no specific organ, unlike the other five well-known senses.

E1019.name: interaction design
E1019.text: interaction design; also called: interaction design and modeling. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world. The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

E1020.name: perceptual design
E1020.text: perceptual design; also called: perceptual design and modeling. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

E1021.name: modeling
E1021.text: modeling. The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware requires proper interaction design and modeling for the user's interaction with input devices, perceptual design and modeling so that stimuli generated by output devices suitably stimulate the user's sense organs, and software to process input data and generate output data.

E1022.name: virtual reality engine
E1022.text: virtual reality engine; also called: VR engine. A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer. In a layered virtual reality (VR) system, a developer can rely on the software development kit (SDK) layer to access the VR engine; the developer has to install the VR engine and import the SDK within the engine, and the VR engine's job is to let the developer deal with graphics through the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by the native rendering libraries without directly accessing those native rendering libraries.

E1023.name: software-and-database component
E1023.text: software-and-database component. The software part of the virtual reality (VR) data-flow diagram is represented by two components: the virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

E1024.name: environment modeling
E1024.text: environment modeling; also called: object modeling. Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

E1025.name: stereoscopic output view
E1025.text: stereoscopic output view; also called: view. Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware. In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses. From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

E1026.name: high-level description
E1026.text: high-level description. Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware. In practice, a virtual reality (VR) developer may need to implement much functionality from scratch instead of providing only high-level descriptions that software automatically converts to low-level details.

E1027.text: low-level detail. Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware. In practice, a virtual reality (VR) developer may need to implement much functionality from scratch instead of providing only high-level descriptions that software automatically converts to low-level details.

E1028.name: software library
E1028.text: software library; also called: library, software libraries. Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware. ARToolKit is one of the most widely adopted software libraries for developing augmented reality (AR) applications; it is written in C and supports platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS. To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support. When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking. Open Scene Graph (OSG) is an open-source scene graph library, Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) is an open-source successor of OSG, and both are widely used.

E1029.name: platform
E1029.text: platform. In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them. Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device. In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms. A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms. Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

E1030.name: operating system
E1030.text: operating system; also called: OS. In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them. In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms. A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms. The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions. In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the stimuli were rendered on a 64-bit computer running Windows 11 Professional operating system (OS), equipped with a 3.6 GHz quad-core processor and a 4GB GeForce GTX 1080 graphics processing unit (GPU).

E1031.name: device driver
E1031.text: device driver. In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

E1032.name: display output
E1032.text: display output. In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

E1033.name: game engine
E1033.text: game engine; also called: virtual reality engine, VR engine. A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed. Using a game engine as middleware can avoid substantial initial effort but may be cumbersome for implementing ideas not part of standard video games, and if the engine is not specifically a virtual reality (VR) engine, the developer loses some flexibility. A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions. A game engine is a software development environment for building extended reality (XR) experiences, and a developer can build their own application on top of it. A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising multiple components, for example a physics engine, a rendering engine, an audio engine, and a user interface.

E1034.name: virtual world generator
E1034.text: virtual world generator; also called: VWG. The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered. The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically. The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match. The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

E1035.name: black box
E1035.text: black box. The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.

E1036.name: head tracker
E1036.text: head tracker. The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

E1037.name: head position
E1037.text: head position. The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically. Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. A virtual ray in pointing-based selection is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.

E1042.text: renderer; also called: output renderer. E1050.name: triangular mesh
E1050.text: triangular mesh; also called: mesh, triangular meshes. Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input. Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.

E1051.text: material surface property; also called: material and physical surface properties. A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

E1053.name: light
E1053.text: light. A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces. Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate. Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light. The photon (particle) view of light describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles that move through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and it is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor. The wave view of light describes light as waves, ripples through space, and it is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

E1054.name: sound
E1054.text: sound. Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum. Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low. Pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience, because pressure at the human eardrum varies as a function of time. Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses. Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.

E1055.name: force

Kinesthesis is the awareness of the parameters associated with moving body parts, and it provides information on velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement. In Unity, a joint connects a rigid body to another rigid body or to a fixed point in space, can apply forces that move the rigid bodies, has limits that restrict that movement, and can be used to model the realistic movement of specific objects or characters such as a ball and socket joint like a hip or shoulder, any skeletal joint, doors, finger joints, or a piece of elastic.

E1056.name: computer graphics
E1056.text: computer graphics; also called: CG. Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations. One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support. For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support. In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen. The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

E1061.name: matched motion
E1061.text: matched motion. Matched motion in virtual reality (VR) is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world. In virtual reality (VR), the real-world motions reflected in the virtual world vary among virtual reality experiences: head motions must be matched so the visual renderer uses the correct viewpoint, and other body parts require tracking and matched motion when the user needs hand-eye coordination or looks at those body parts during the experience. Virtual reality (VR) software should include developer support for resolving matched-motion challenges, such as deciding which real-world motions to reflect and creating a correspondence between a user's physical motion in the matched zone and a different virtual motion. User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone.

E1062.name: obstacle mismatch
E1062.text: obstacle mismatch. In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

E1065.name: user locomotion
E1065.text: user locomotion. User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone. A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor. Support for user locomotion, including different sorts of locomotion so that cyber sickness can be addressed, should be part of virtual reality (VR) software.

E1066.name: locomotion operation
E1066.text: locomotion operation. Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement. Virtual reality (VR) locomotion operations that let the user avoid physical movement may lead to cyber sickness, which increases with exposure duration and other factors.

E1068.name: physics support
E1068.text: physics support. Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator, in addition to computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, locomotion support, and matched motion support. The basic purpose of physics support in a virtual world generator is to make the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, so that events observed in the real world have similar events in the virtual world. Physics support in a virtual world generator should make a dropped ball accelerate toward the ground due to gravity rather than move it at constant speed. Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

A rigid body in Unity is a concept and a property that, when attached to a game object, allows the game object to respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing from a surface appears realistic in accordance with everyday experience. The isKinematic property, used with a Unity rigid body, can remove the object from physics engine control and allow it to be moved kinematically from a script, so it does not automatically follow gravity, and the developer can choose whether the object follows gravity.

Within the shared virtual world of a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience, user interactions, including collisions, must be managed by the virtual reality system whether users are close or spread around the world. When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required. A ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) or higher-level engine makes it easy for developers to create a virtual reality (VR) experience in little time because it comes with supports, including support for collisions or physics, so the developer does not have to build things from scratch. A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

E1079.name: surface
E1079.text: surface. Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate. Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved. Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed. Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used. In mesh representation, a greater number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces but makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained.

E1080.name: light source
E1080.text: light source; also called: sources of light, source, light sources, light. A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived. In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface. In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

The images and videos, mostly the images, were edited with image editing tools for uniform illumination because the 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another will make the user feel that something is odd.

E1082.name: smell
E1082.text: smell; also called: scent. The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose). Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli. There is much less research on integrating smell and taste into extended reality (XR) systems than on visual, auditory, and touch senses, and fewer electronic devices have been made or are being made to provide stimuli to the nose and tongue, the body organs responsible for smell and taste. Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama.

E1083.name: networked collaborative virtual reality experience
E1083.text: networked collaborative virtual reality experience. A networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere. In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, each user has a distinct matched zone; matched zones may overlap in the real world, but most often they are disjoint and distributed around the Earth, so unwanted physical collision must be avoided when users are close, while users spread around the globe have no possibility of physical collision. Within the shared virtual world of a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience, user interactions, including collisions, must be managed by the virtual reality system whether users are close or spread around the world. In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

E1089.name: driver
E1089.text: driver; also called: basic drivers. A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

E1090.name: application programming interface
E1090.text: application programming interface; also called: API, interfaces, APIs. A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements. The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks. The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application.

E1093.name: locomotion
E1093.text: locomotion; also called: travel, travel part of navigation. The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is the motor component of navigation and refers to the actual movement between two locations. Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place. Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination. Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

E1096.name: lighting model
E1096.text: lighting model; also called: simple lighting model. In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception. In computer graphics, lighting models and shading models are distinct, although they may physically represent more or less similar things, and they are differentiated by the computation involved: lighting models involve more computation than shading models, and shading models are used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience. Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, and they rely on lighting models. Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values. In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point.

Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

E1098.name: OpenSimulator
E1098.text: OpenSimulator. OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

E1101.name: application software
E1101.text: application software; also called: higher-level application software, application software products. A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions. In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory. User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable. The extended reality (XR) application software being developed is interactive software intended for laypersons, who may not know or need to know how the hardware or software works. Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

E1103.name: software development environment
E1103.text: software development environment. A game engine is a software development environment for building extended reality (XR) experiences, and a developer can build their own application on top of it.

E1104.name: physics engine
E1104.text: physics engine. A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime. The rendering, audio, and physics engines are often basic components of a game engine, but not all game engines contain all of these components.

E1105.name: rendering engine
E1105.text: rendering engine. A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform. A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU). The rendering, audio, and physics engines are often basic components of a game engine, but not all game engines contain all of these components.

E1106.name: audio engine
E1106.text: audio engine. An audio engine is a part of basic game engine support that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system. An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering. An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio. The rendering, audio, and physics engines are often basic components of a game engine, but not all game engines contain all of these components.

E1107.name: user interface
E1107.text: user interface; also called: user interfaces. A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising multiple components, for example a physics engine, a rendering engine, an audio engine, and a user interface. Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases. The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery. Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable. Interface issues include an external system interface, meaning interfacing between hardware and software, and a user interface, where usability issues arise.

E1108.name: authoring tool
E1108.text: authoring tool. An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine. An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment.

E1109.name: scripting
E1109.text: scripting. An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment. Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management. In Unity, scripting supports user interaction with input devices through inbuilt handling of inputs such as the mouse, keyboard, and buttons; for other device-specific inputs, imported software development kit (SDK) input support may be needed and it extends Unity's inbuilt support. Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems are primarily programming tasks, with the amount of programming depending on the required functionality: a basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment (IDE) support, whereas a customized experience requires scripting, which involves more programming.

E1121.name: rasterization
E1121.text: rasterization. In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.

E1123.name: Direct3D
E1123.text: Direct3D. A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU). Examples of graphics libraries include OpenGL, which stands for Open Graphics Library, Vulkan, and Direct3D. A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

The major native graphics libraries supported by Unity are DirectX, which is primarily in the Windows environment, Metal for Apple systems, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), and Vulkan, and many other native graphics libraries are also supported. For this sample project, the Unity player settings are configured under Edit > Project Settings > Player > Other by removing Vulkan and adding the Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) application programming interface (API), unchecking AutoGraphics API, unchecking Advanced RISC Machines (ARM) version 7, checking ARM 64, using the IL2CPP scripting backend, and ensuring the minimum API level is greater than 7; these settings are application-specific and may not work for other projects or platforms.

E1140.name: deployment
E1140.text: deployment; also called: publish, deploy. Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device. In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms. Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance. E1143.name: Windows
E1143.text: Windows; also called: window, normalized clipping window, view plane. A window is the same as a normalized clipping window, is another term for the view plane, and is an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display. A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy). In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

E1193.name: augmented reality software tool
E1193.text: augmented reality software tool; also called: AR software tools. Augmented Reality (AR) software tools can be categorized by developer skill, target application platform (desktop AR applications or mobile AR applications), or tracking technology (computer vision (CV)-based tracking or other sensors such as Global Positioning System (GPS) sensors). In a skill-based hierarchy, Augmented Reality (AR) software tools are arranged in four categories according to decreasing programming skill: low-level software libraries or frameworks, rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools. The skill requirements for the four skill-based Augmented Reality (AR) software tool categories are: low-level software libraries or frameworks require strong programming or coding ability and understanding of how to call the library functions; rapid prototyping tools require some programming ability, lower than for low-level tools, and may require design prototyping skills; plugins require skill with the original developer tool with which the plugin is used; and standalone AR authoring tools assume no programming ability and can be used without any knowledge. Examples of Augmented Reality (AR) software tools for each skill-based category are: AR Toolkit, OSG Art, StudiersTube, and MXR Toolkit for low-level software libraries or frameworks; FLAR Manager and OpenFrameworks for rapid prototyping tools; AR media plugins, Vuforia, MetaIO Unity plugins, and Dart for plugins for existing developer tools; and BuildAR, MetaIO Creator, and Wikitude for standalone AR authoring tools.

Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring. Plugins to existing tools provide an easy and quick method for developing augmented reality (AR) applications when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, because the developer can rely on knowledge of the original tool and only needs to understand the plugin, reducing the required understanding of the system; if the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch.

Vuforia is an augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking. Vuforia is a software development kit (SDK) specifically developed for augmented reality (AR) that supports advanced computer vision functionality for recognizing images and objects and interacting with spaces in the real world. Vuforia is a cross-platform software development kit (SDK) that supports multiple platforms, including Unity, Android, and iOS, and using it requires a license, with a developer's license available. To install Vuforia in Unity, a new Unity project is created using the universal 3D template or an empty project, and the Vuforia engine is added to the project assets either by downloading the Vuforia SDK for Unity from developer.vuforia.com or by manually importing the package as a custom package, after which it can be used directly in the Unity editor.

E1221.name: Wikitude
E1221.text: Wikitude. Wikitude is a free augmented reality (AR) browser application that runs on mobile devices as a useful mobile prototyping tool. Wikitude treats the mobile device primarily as a client or rendering device only, and the application connects to backend servers for content and specification of user interface elements, with computation not taking place on the mobile device but possibly taking place on the backend server. Wikitude makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, developers depend on default content provided by the tool, which may reduce flexibility but is still usable.

E1222.name: low-level library and framework
E1222.text: low-level library and framework. Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

E1223.name: C
E1223.text: C. ARToolKit is one of the most widely adopted software libraries for developing augmented reality (AR) applications; it is written in C and supports platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS.

E1224.name: Linux

E1225.name: marker-based tracking
E1225.text: marker-based tracking. ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques. In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position.

E1226.name: ARToolWorks
E1226.text: ARToolWorks; also called: AR Tool Works. ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques. The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

E1227.name: natural feature
E1227.text: natural feature. ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.

E1228.name: OpenGL
E1228.text: OpenGL; also called: Open Graphics Library. ARToolKit provides only low-level OpenGL-based rendering support, with very primitive rendering and no built-in support for interaction techniques or complex realistic graphics, so using it alone yields a rudimentary system in which the developer must write interaction from scratch, making a complete realistic augmented reality (AR) application difficult and time-consuming. Open Scene Graph (OSG) and similar scene-graph libraries are written in C++ and are built on top of OpenGL, which accesses lower-level hardware. Examples of graphics libraries include OpenGL, which stands for Open Graphics Library, Vulkan, and Direct3D. A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

E1229.name: augmented reality toolkit
E1229.text: augmented reality toolkit; also called: AR toolkit. Many standard augmented reality (AR) toolkits or low-level libraries primarily provide tracking support but lack the features needed for realistic rendering of digital content over the real-world view and for interaction support. FLAR Toolkit is a version of the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash and allows an AR experience to be run from within a web browser. For augmented reality (AR) application development, Open Frameworks provides support for tracking, rendering, and interaction, and can combine more than two libraries, for example a tracking library such as augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for hand tracking, a three-dimensional (3D) scene graph for rendering, and audio playback libraries, to generate different effects.

E1230.name: framework
E1230.text: framework. Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application. To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support. Examples of frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries include the Open Scene Graph (OSG) ART 3 library, which links ARToolKit for tracking support with OSG for real-time rendering features; Goblin XNA, which combines the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform; and Metaio SDK plus OSG, in which the Metaio SDK provides augmented reality (AR) tracking technologies and OSG provides rendering support. Mobile-specific augmented reality (AR) frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia; DroidAR uses other sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support.

E1231.name: scene graph
E1231.text: scene graph. A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application. Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality. When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking. Open Scene Graph (OSG) is an open-source scene graph library, Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) is an open-source successor of OSG, and both are widely used. Open Scene Graph (OSG) and similar scene-graph libraries are written in C++ and are built on top of OpenGL, which accesses lower-level hardware.

E1232.name: node
E1232.text: node; also called: vertex, point of interest. A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application. In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect. In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time. In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number. For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

E1233.text: computer graphics scene; also called: AR scene. E1234.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
E1234.text: three-dimensional graphics pipeline; also called: 3D graphics pipeline. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion. The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system. The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

E1236.name: clipping
E1236.text: clipping. Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality. Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection. To project a point P from the world coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view plane, P is first transformed to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, then the view volume containing P is transformed to a canonical view volume before clipping, and finally the point in the canonical view volume is projected onto the view plane; the final point P' is obtained by multiplying P by the world coordinate system to three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system transformation matrix, the canonical view volume transformation matrix, and the projection transformation matrix. Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix. A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

E1254.name: library
E1254.text: library. Flash augmented reality (AR) Manager (FLAR Manager) is a framework that combines various augmented reality tracking and graphics libraries, primarily for prototyping. In Flash augmented reality Manager (FLAR Manager), an augmented reality tracking library such as FLAR Toolkit or FLAR Tracker can be combined with a three-dimensional (3D) graphics library such as Alternative 3D, Away 3D, Away 3D Lite, Paper Vision 3D, or Sandy 3D, and such combinations are used primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development. E1255.name: prototype
E1255.text: prototype; also called: prototypes, fast prototype. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized. Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle. Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas. A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first. A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

E1257.name: flar toolkit
E1257.text: flar toolkit. Adobe Flash is a popular authoring tool for creating prototypes with multimedia content for web and desktop platforms and can be used, through augmented reality (AR) plugins such as FLAR Toolkit or Flash AR Manager (FLAR Manager), to prototype desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences. FLAR Toolkit is a version of the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash and allows an AR experience to be run from within a web browser. FLAR Toolkit lets a user, with a few lines of code, activate a camera, track augmented reality (AR) markers in the camera view, and load and overlay virtual content onto the tracked image for three-dimensional (3D) registering. FLAR Toolkit makes it possible for anyone with a Flash-enabled web browser and a camera connected to a computer to have or develop an augmented reality (AR) experience with minimal effort because the required tracking and overlay activities can be done with a few lines of code. In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. In the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development, functional and non-functional requirements, including usability requirements, are collected from end users and clients, who may be the same but are usually different; usability requirements primarily come from end users, other non-functional requirements may come from clients, and functional requirements may come from both clients and end users. The traditional interactive system development lifecycle is rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts and before deployment; for example, all requirements must be identified before the requirement gathering stage is complete and all units must be coded before the coding stage is sent to testing; this strict stage completion can lead to time and cost overruns and even non-acceptance by the client.

Wikitude makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, developers depend on default content provided by the tool, which may reduce flexibility but is still usable. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly. In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

E1289.name: plugin to existing tools
E1289.text: plugin to existing tools; also called: plugins to existing tools. Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring. Plugins to existing tools provide an easy and quick method for developing augmented reality (AR) applications when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, because the developer can rely on knowledge of the original tool and only needs to understand the plugin, reducing the required understanding of the system; if the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch. Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases. A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level augmented reality (AR) tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool, an approach that applies to any higher-level tool.

E1295.name: Unity
E1295.text: Unity; also called: Unity platform, Unity development environment, Unity environment. Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems. The Unity platform comprises the Unity three-dimensional (3D) game engine and a developer's interface that a developer can use to implement ideas. The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline. Unity is a cross-platform game engine that Unity Technologies initially released in 2005. Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

E1307.name: standalone authoring tool
E1307.text: standalone authoring tool; also called: standalone augmented reality authoring tools. Standalone authoring tools are applications that allow users to create augmented reality (AR) experiences without programming experience. Unlike plugins, which require a basic software or basic authoring tool on which augmented reality (AR) support is provided through a plugin, standalone authoring tools are complete packages that include content authoring and augmented reality support and do not require or depend on any other tool. Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior. Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them. Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools can provide scripting-language support for developers who know scripting languages, and applications built with absolute zero coding have limited utility compared with advanced systems that use scripting support for more flexibility.

E1309.name: animation
E1309.text: animation; also called: animations. Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior. Wikitude Studio is an example of a standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tool; it is a web-based package that allowed users to create rich mobile augmented reality content and deploy it either to the Wikitude augmented reality browser app or as a custom mobile app, and it supported various media, including three-dimensional (3D) models and animations registered to the real world. The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation. A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters. In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold.

Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces. Some design guidelines are generic, small in number, and cover broad high-level aspects of interactive systems; examples are Shneiderman's eight golden rules and Donald Norman's seven principles, both primarily intended for graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but applicable to other domains, with Norman's seven principles developed in the 1980s. Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules originally developed in 1986 primarily for graphical user interfaces (GUIs), and can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality (XR) systems. Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.
