E1317.name: extended reality system
E1317.text: extended reality system; also called: XR system, XR systems, extended reality systems. Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

E1318.name: interactive system
E1318.text: interactive system; also called: interactive systems. Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of systems called interactive systems. The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that. Empirical or field studies of user behavior are typically needed to understand who the users of an interactive system are and how they behave, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so interactive-system designers can rely on the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with field studies. A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time. Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.

E1319.name: disappearing technology
names: the most profound technologies are those that disappear
E1319.text: disappearing technology; also called: the most profound technologies are those that disappear. Mark Weiser's 1991 paper 'The Computer for the 21st Century', published in Scientific American, stated that the most profound technologies are those that disappear. The statement that the most profound technologies are those that disappear means that a very advanced technology should ideally not be visible to the user, and the user should feel like dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item. Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product. In the development of computer systems, people have tried to make technology disappear from the user's point of view, and the current stage defined by popular technological products such as wearable devices, mobile devices, flexible devices, and connected devices is referred to as Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing, in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear.

E1326.name: interactive computing system
E1326.text: interactive computing system; also called: interactive system, interactive computing systems. Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user. In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works. Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

E1327.name: lay person
E1327.text: lay person; also called: layman user, lay end user, layperson, laypersons. In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works. Technical terms in a system error message, such as event log, security accounts manager, and safe mode, should not be expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user, and a hexadecimal status code in such a message is generally incomprehensible to a layperson. An error message couched in technical jargon that a layperson is likely to fail to understand can make the user anxious, leave the user not knowing what is wrong or how to get out of it, and may lead to the user refraining from using the system further and to a loss of motivation for further use. E1333.text: user-centric approach. The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that. The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

E1334.name: user characteristic
E1334.text: user characteristic; also called: user characteristics, users' characteristics. The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that. Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome. The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery. An application software developer building software such as a virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) system incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations so that the system is easier for the user to use and better matches the users' needs and expectations. Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users of computers, so such user characteristics must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules originally developed in 1986 primarily for graphical user interfaces (GUIs), and can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality (XR) systems. Interaction for system control is an interaction technique whose goal is to issue commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file, and these commands are most of the regular operations associated with using any software.

E1340.name: human-computer interaction
E1340.text: human-computer interaction; also called: HCI. Human-computer interaction (HCI) is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems. ACM SIGCHI is the official body that deals with human-computer interaction (HCI) and provides the definition of HCI. The core concern of human-computer interaction (HCI) is incorporating humans into the design, which requires first understanding users and then incorporating user characteristics into the design.

The objective of usability requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application is to identify end-user requirements that ensure usability and to specify them so they can be converted into plans for system design, implementation, and deployment. User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group. Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design. Internal consistency in system design means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than using separate objects, elements, or interactions.

E1343.name: field study
E1343.text: field study; also called: empirical studies, field studies. A team collected the Satra graph data through a field study, described as a kind of contextual inquiry, during the Kati Bihu festival, by observing people's travel and stopping behavior throughout the day, manually recording that behavior, and interviewing campus residents and Satra committee members about the places people typically visit and the places interviewees recommended to tourists.

E1344.name: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization
names: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization
E1344.text: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization; also called: three-class classification of interactive-system users. Empirical or field studies of user behavior are typically needed to understand who the users of an interactive system are and how they behave, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so interactive-system designers can rely on the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with field studies. A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time. In the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, an expert user is not a technology expert but a person who is an expert in using the system and can use it efficiently. The novice, intermittent, and expert user classes provide a starting point for understanding users and making interactive-system design decisions when designers assume their potential users belong to one of these classes, because users in different classes are likely to behave differently and designers can broadly understand the behavior of each class. The novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is only one broad way of classifying users; more fine-grained categorizations are possible, and better categorizations can be based on empirical studies of users, but the broad novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is useful when the design process starts.

E1345.name: novice user
E1345.text: novice user; also called: novice first-time users. A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time. For saving a file, the menu option takes longer than the hotkey combination but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be a better alternative for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.

E1357.name: International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard
E1357.text: International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard; also called: ISO 9241-210-2009 standard. The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

E1358.name: effectiveness
E1358.text: effectiveness. The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

E1361.name: context of use
E1361.text: context of use; also called: specified context of use, work context. The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use. The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use. Knowing how users behave in a specific work context is essential to ensure that the software, product, or system being built is usable, because usability is defined with respect to that specific work context. The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements.

E1362.name: user-centered design
E1362.text: user-centered design; also called: user-centered software development approach, user-centered design approach, user-centric design, human-centric design, participatory design, UCD, user-centric. User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application. Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces. The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability. Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process. The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.

E1363.name: design lifecycle
E1363.text: design lifecycle; also called: development lifecycle. User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application. User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable.

E1369.name: user-centric software design
E1369.text: user-centric software design. In user-centric software design and software development, the core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users.

E1370.name: software development
E1370.text: software development. In user-centric software design and software development, the core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users. The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved. A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

E1371.name: software development lifecycle
E1371.text: software development lifecycle; also called: software development life cycle, SDLC. Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner. A software development lifecycle is a systematic, structured set of connected stages for developing and deploying software that comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities needed to build the software. Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages. A software development life cycle (SDLC) is a systematic approach that helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability, because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone. A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence.

E1372.name: extended reality software
E1372.text: extended reality software; also called: XR software. The core concern of Extended Reality (XR) software is to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment, and both software and hardware play important roles in building that relationship. A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage.

E1373.name: xr engine
E1373.text: xr engine. An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

E1374.name: application layer
E1374.text: application layer. An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

E1375.name: input data
E1375.text: input data; also called: device-specific sensory or input data. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

E1376.name: output data
E1376.text: output data. E1378.name: output modeling
E1378.text: output modeling; also called: modeling of output. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

E1379.name: output stimulus
E1379.text: output stimulus; also called: output stimuli. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

E1380.name: perception
E1380.text: perception. The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which is the lowest level, to perception, which is at a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses. The human brain contains around 86 billion neurons, and roughly 20 billion of its neurons are devoted to the cerebral cortex, the part of the brain that is responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness. The brain processes perception by combining signals from multiple senses and proprioception with experiences learned over a long period and interpreting the inputs in coherent, consistent, and familiar learned ways.

E1381.name: perceptual stimuli
E1381.text: perceptual stimuli. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

E1382.name: illusion of reality
E1382.text: illusion of reality. In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world. Creating the best possible illusion of reality is very crucial for virtual reality (VR) because VR aims for total immersion in a virtual environment, whereas in augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) immersion is partial and the real world remains viewable or experienced, so the illusion is less significant but not totally insignificant.

E1383.name: perceptual system
E1383.text: perceptual system. A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.

E1384.name: artificial stimulation
E1384.text: artificial stimulation; also called: virtual reality stimulation. Human bodies and sensory organs are designed to perceive the real world, not a virtual world, and applying artificial stimulation in virtual reality affects biological mechanisms that evolved over a long period in a natural environment. Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior. One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system. Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

E1386.name: physiology
E1386.text: physiology. Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory. Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of the basic physiology of the human body, including sense organs, neural pathways, and how they are connected to the brain; the key theories and insights of experimental perceptual psychology; and the interference of an engineered extended reality (XR) system with common perceptual processes, with its implications or side effects.

E1387.name: long-term memory
E1387.text: long-term memory. Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory. In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification. In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

E1391.name: perceptual psychology
E1391.text: perceptual psychology. Perceptual psychology is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation, received by sensors from the real world, into perceived phenomena. Having a little bit of knowledge of perceptual psychology is always advisable for interactive systems in general and is even more important for extended reality (XR) systems because the goal of extended reality systems is to explicitly extend the user's deeply embedded idea of reality. Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for building better hardware and for understanding the effects of an extended reality (XR) system on the user by answering questions such as how far away an object appears in a given virtual world, how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, whether the user's head appears at the proper height in the virtual world for the point of view that should correspond to the user's height, where virtual sound appears to come from, why a user feels nauseated, why one system experience is more tiring than another, and what presence is. Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of the basic physiology of the human body, including sense organs, neural pathways, and how they are connected to the brain; the key theories and insights of experimental perceptual psychology; and the interference of an engineered extended reality (XR) system with common perceptual processes, with its implications or side effects.

E1393.name: pixel
E1393.text: pixel; also called: pixels, picture element, picture elements. A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen. The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s. In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing. In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.

The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions. E1404.text: receptor; also called: receptors, sense organ receptors. Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ. Different types of receptors include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors. The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis. Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.

E1405.name: vision
E1405.text: vision. E1425.text: visible light; also called: visible light waves, visible light spectrum. E1454.text: input edge; also called: input edges. The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

E1456.name: synapse
E1456.text: synapse. For an interconnection between neurons, an axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next neuron, but the axon and dendrite are not physically connected; communication occurs across a gap called the synapse, through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

E1458.name: synaptic connection
E1458.text: synaptic connection; also called: synaptic connections. In the human brain, each neuron has on average about 7,000 synaptic connections to other neurons, which results in about 10^15 edges in the brain's neuron-interconnection graph.

E1459.name: edge
E1459.text: edge. The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

E1460.name: hierarchical processing
E1460.text: hierarchical processing. Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex. Hierarchical processing works by staged aggregation, in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached, and aggregated information at each level is higher-level information rather than the same lower-level information. Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

E1464.name: sensory input
E1464.text: sensory input; also called: sensory signals, real-time sensory input. In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification. Overall perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience.

E1465.name: interpretation of a stimulus
E1465.text: interpretation of a stimulus. In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification. The interpretation of a stimulus depends on the interpreter's long-term experience, so a person with less experience such as a newborn and a person with long experience such as an aged person can interpret a stimulus very differently.

E1471.name: proprioception
E1471.text: proprioception; also called: sixth sense. Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense. The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis. Proprioception, called the sixth sense, is the conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable human body part, such as legs, arms, fingers, tongue, mouth, and lips, relative to other body parts. The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis. The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

E1472.name: muscular effort
E1472.text: muscular effort. The motor cortex, which controls body motion, sends signals called efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort required to move them.

E1477.text: visual input. Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

E1478.name: retina
E1478.text: retina. Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye. The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina. The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain. The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea. The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

E1481.name: light propagation
E1481.text: light propagation. Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception. Knowledge of the physics of light propagation is used to understand the construction of virtual worlds by modeling light propagation and determining what should be rendered on visual displays. Knowledge of how light propagates, how lenses and the eye work, and how cameras work is used to understand camera setups, choose camera positions in virtual worlds for the best experience, and present virtual worlds through panoramic videos.

E1482.name: visual perception
E1482.text: visual perception. Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception. The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain. In a virtual desert walking example, visual and auditory perception alone may not give a complete picture of the haptic touch perception of feeling sand glide under the feet, and adding haptic exploration support through proper hardware and software makes the experience far better than an experience using only visual or auditory senses.

E1487.name: photon view
E1487.text: photon view; also called: particle view. Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light. The photon (particle) view of light describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles that move through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and it is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

E1488.name: wave view
E1488.text: wave view. Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light. The wave view of light describes light as waves, ripples through space, and it is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

E1489.name: ray view

The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

E1497.name: light ray
E1497.text: light ray. When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur. In light transmission, some of the light rays that strike a material surface pass through the material and come out of the material. In absorption, some of the light rays that strike a material surface are absorbed by the material, terminate inside the material, and do not propagate further outside the material. In reflection, a light ray strikes a material surface and is reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating the material.

E1502.name: color perception
E1502.text: color perception. In color perception, the perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye. Color is perceived only in photopic vision, which is accomplished with cones and gives a sense of color, whereas in scotopic vision weak lights are perceived as a series of grays and color perception is not that good. Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing photopic vision, which is color perception, while light waves outside the visible light spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception. Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

E1503.name: perceived color
E1503.text: perceived color. In color perception, the perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.

E1504.name: intensity
E1504.text: intensity; also called: light intensity. A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived. In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point. In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

E1505.name: ambient light
E1505.text: ambient light. Ambient light is light in the environment, reflected from surrounding objects, that reaches the viewer's eye together with light reflected from the object's surface.

E1506.name: cornea
E1506.text: cornea. Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye. The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina. The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves. In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index. The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

E1511.name: optic nerve fiber
E1511.text: optic nerve fiber; also called: optic nerve fibers. The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain. Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

E1512.name: rod
E1512.text: rod; also called: rods. The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea. Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity. Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

E1513.name: cone
E1513.text: cone; also called: cones. The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea. Color is perceived only in photopic vision, which is accomplished with cones and gives a sense of color, whereas in scotopic vision weak lights are perceived as a series of grays and color perception is not that good.

E1514.name: fovea
E1514.text: fovea. The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea. The fovea is the central region of the retina with the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, particularly cones. The innermost part of the fovea has a diameter of only 0.5 millimeters or an angular range of 0.85 plus or minus 0.85 degrees and contains almost entirely cones.

E1515.name: image acuity
E1515.text: image acuity. Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

E1516.name: photopic vision

E1517.name: central vision
E1517.text: central vision. Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly. Central vision requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image. Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

E1518.name: scotopic vision
E1518.text: scotopic vision. Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision. E1519.name: peripheral vision
E1519.text: peripheral vision. Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly. Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones. Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

E1520.name: spectrum
E1520.text: spectrum. Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

E1521.name: frequency
E1521.text: frequency; also called: frequencies, sound frequency. Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave. Frequency of a sound wave is the number of alterations between one maximum and another maximum per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The human audible frequency range, which is a limitation of human physiology, is from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 hertz, and frequencies inside this range are audible to a human ear while frequencies outside this range are not, although other animals can perceive a higher range outside the human range.

E1522.name: electromagnetic light wave
E1522.text: electromagnetic light wave; also called: light waves. E1524.text: hertz; also called: Hz. For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

E1528.name: photoreceptor density
E1528.text: photoreceptor density. Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly. Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones. Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.

E1529.name: angular range
E1529.text: angular range. The innermost part of the fovea has a diameter of only 0.5 millimeters or an angular range of 0.85 plus or minus 0.85 degrees and contains almost entirely cones.

E1530.name: rod density

E1532.name: blind spot
E1532.text: blind spot. The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

E1536.name: natural lens
E1536.text: natural lens; also called: lens. The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves. The interior of the human eye is liquid, so after transmission through the lens light passes through liquid, whereas in an artificially created lens setup light passes through air after the lens. In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index. The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

E1539.text: lens setup; also called: artificially created lens setup. Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum. Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

E1545.text: diopter. Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina. A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.

E1548.name: engineered lens
E1548.text: engineered lens. For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

E1549.name: focal length
E1549.text: focal length. For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

E1550.name: virtual image
E1550.text: virtual image. For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

E1551.name: real image
E1551.text: real image. In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

E1552.name: view frustum
E1552.text: view frustum. Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

E1553.name: horizontal field of view
E1553.text: horizontal field of view; also called: FOV. The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

E1554.name: vertical field of view
E1554.text: vertical field of view. The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

E1555.name: binocular vision
E1555.text: binocular vision. In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye. Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space. When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

E1556.name: left eye
E1556.text: left eye. In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye. Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

E1557.name: right eye
E1557.text: right eye. In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye. Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

E1558.name: depth perception
E1558.text: depth perception. Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space.

E1559.name: stereoscopy
E1559.text: stereoscopy. Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

E1560.name: three-dimensional view
E1560.text: three-dimensional view; also called: 3D view. When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

E1561.name: translational movement
E1561.text: translational movement. A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

E1562.name: rotational movement
E1562.text: rotational movement. A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

E1563.name: degree of freedom
E1563.text: degree of freedom; also called: degrees of freedom. The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space. In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes. In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

E1564.name: six degrees of freedom

E1568.name: human visual sense
E1568.text: human visual sense; also called: visual sense. Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors. To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

E1569.text: spatial resolution. To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter. E1574.name: aliasing
E1574.text: aliasing. Aliasing in a display is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible, such as when the display is highly magnified or zoomed out. To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution. Aliasing is distortion that may occur in an original shape after scan conversion because scan conversion renders pixels that are close to points on the original shape rather than exactly rendering the points, so an approximated line may not exactly match the original line. If aliasing is left unaddressed, it may lead to distortion that is visible with a change in resolution and that will reduce the quality of experience. Anti-aliasing operations are additional operations, using complex algorithms, that remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing so that the end effect is better.

E1575.name: screen door effect
E1575.text: screen door effect. The screen door effect is an effect, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display (LCD) projectors, in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it. To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

E1576.name: retina display
E1576.text: retina display. A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display. For augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays and virtual reality (VR) headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye, the traditional 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion is not very suitable; a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch (ppi) is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.

E1577.text: pixels per linear inch; also called: ppi. E1584.name: immersive environment
E1584.text: immersive environment; also called: immersive environments. Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience. Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

E1585.name: audio component
E1585.text: audio component; also called: audio, auditory effects, auditory experience. The audio component of virtual reality (VR) is powerful for providing an immersive experience, and technologies exist to bring high-fidelity audio into VR, so using those technologies will clearly improve the immersive experience. The objective in dealing with an immersive experience is to include as many senses as possible, because the visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, which will affect the immersive experience, and augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience. Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version. Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects. Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness. For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized. The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene. E1595.name: material
E1595.text: material; also called: materials. A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data. In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape. In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

E1596.text: distance; also called: D. For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized. The corridor experiment used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances of 20, 20, 13, 16, 6.4, 19, and 4 meters from the start. Participants were instructed to start walking from the starting place and stop at each painting to click a photograph, a task assigned to ensure that the user stopped after walking a predefined distance. In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

E1597.name: virtual experience
E1597.text: virtual experience. Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve. Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment. The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

E1601.name: propagation
E1601.text: propagation. Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum. Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

E1603.name: pressure variation
E1603.text: pressure variation. Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low. Pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience, because pressure at the human eardrum varies as a function of time. Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses.

E1607.name: sound wave
E1607.text: sound wave. Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses. Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave. Frequency of a sound wave is the number of alterations between one maximum and another maximum per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave, measured in decibel (dB) relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 hertz (Hz). Phase of a sound wave is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin from 0 to 360 degrees, and is measured in degrees.

E1608.name: human audible frequency range
E1608.text: human audible frequency range; also called: human range. The human audible frequency range, which is a limitation of human physiology, is from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 hertz, and frequencies inside this range are audible to a human ear while frequencies outside this range are not, although other animals can perceive a higher range outside the human range.

E1613.name: human hearing system
E1613.text: human hearing system. The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

E1614.name: outer ear
E1614.text: outer ear. The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear. In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies. The complex folds in the outer ear's receiver part and outer-ear canal attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

E1615.name: middle ear
E1615.text: middle ear. The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear. In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

E1616.name: inner ear
E1616.text: inner ear. The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear. The inner ear houses the cochlea, which is the sense organ for hearing, in a structure the size of a marble.

E1626.text: cochlea. The inner ear houses the cochlea, which is the sense organ for hearing, in a structure the size of a marble. The cochlea is connected to nerves or neurons and converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

E1629.name: sound perception
E1629.text: sound perception. Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings. Social-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals. Warning-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event. Primitive-level sound perception is the intuitive perception of naive sounds such as background noises that people mostly ignore, and it may not lead to any meaningful action by the individual.

E1630.name: social-level sound perception
E1630.text: social-level sound perception; also called: social, social-level perception. Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings. Social-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals. Identifying the desired sound perception level helps a developer generate suitable auditory effects when generating sound effects for a virtual reality (VR) system; for example, if social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

E1635.name: psychophysics
E1635.text: psychophysics. Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli. Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics and is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by acoustic stimuli or sound. Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units. The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials. Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.

E1639.name: Stevens' power law
E1639.text: Stevens' power law. Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units. Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli. For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

E1642.name: just noticeable difference
E1642.text: just noticeable difference; also called: JND. The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials. Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C. For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, it must be above the just noticeable difference (JND); for it not to be perceived, it must be within or below the JND. For sound frequency, the just noticeable difference (JND) increases as frequency increases: for frequencies less than 1000 Hz, humans can detect a frequency change of less than 1 Hz; at 10,000 Hz the JND is about 100 Hz; in percentage terms, at low frequencies humans can detect frequency differences of 0.1% or less, whereas at higher frequencies a difference of at least 1% is required.
