E1649.name: sound localization
E1649.text: sound localization; also called: localization. Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it. Sound localization is crucial in virtual reality (VR) because it helps the user perceive the orientation and position of objects relative to the user by matching auditory and visual cues; a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness. The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference (JND) concept to sound localization and represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin. The minimum audible angle (MAA) depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source: at some frequencies and locations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at other combinations localization can be very difficult and the MAA can be extremely high.

E1650.name: sound source
E1650.text: sound source; also called: source. Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it. The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source. The minimum audible angle (MAA) depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source: at some frequencies and locations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at other combinations localization can be very difficult and the MAA can be extremely high.

On the minimap, white dots represent the arrangement of the 360-degree images; the user navigates by moving from one image to another along the dots, and the arrangement provides direction and orientation; the user's current image is highlighted green.

E1657.name: sound localization cue
E1657.text: sound localization cue. Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears. Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming. Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.

E1661.name: acoustic shadow
E1661.text: acoustic shadow. An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.

E1663.name: auditory component
E1663.text: auditory component. The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.

E1664.name: head-related transfer function
E1664.text: head-related transfer function; also called: HRTF. Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems. Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, and every person has a unique HRTF. Because every person has a unique head-related transfer function (HRTF), it is impractical to determine individual users' HRTFs when building a system, so an HRTF for an average listener is developed and used. A pair of head-related transfer functions (HRTF) for both ears can be used to synthesize binaural sound, and by generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality (XR) system.

E1665.name: binaural sound

E1666.text: human somatosensory system. The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis. The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis. The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles. The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions. When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense.

E1695.name: haptic perception
E1695.text: haptic perception; also called: haptic touch perception. Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception, and it is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects as part of touch perception. Haptic perception can be thought of at different levels: receptors in the skin receive input from the real world and process the information to perceive something through touch, while higher-level perception requires object manipulations that are called haptic explorations. Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and because mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience, haptic perception can improve an immersive experience. Haptic perception and haptic exploration offer an extra dimension to virtual reality (VR) by letting users feel the virtual environment through the sense of touch, which gives users a better feeling of the virtual world and helps them feel truly immersed in the virtual world, and because immersion in the real world also involves haptic exploration, adding haptic exploration to a virtual world increases the immersive experience. In a virtual desert walking example, visual and auditory perception alone may not give a complete picture of the haptic touch perception of feeling sand glide under the feet, and adding haptic exploration support through proper hardware and software makes the experience far better than an experience using only visual or auditory senses.

E1698.name: haptic exploration
E1698.text: haptic exploration; also called: object manipulations, in-hand manipulation. Haptic exploration is the handling or manipulation of geometric objects that is used to infer the overall geometric shape of the object. Haptic perception can be thought of at different levels: receptors in the skin receive input from the real world and process the information to perceive something through touch, while higher-level perception requires object manipulations that are called haptic explorations. The six types of haptic exploration, each needed for a different object property perception, are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape or volume perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception. Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information. The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object. The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

In the minimum-time approach, the virtual world is represented as a graph whose nodes are points of interest, whose directly connected edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest, and whose graph need not be complete. In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.

E1718.name: mental model
E1718.text: mental model; also called: cognitive map, mental map. Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and because mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience, haptic perception can improve an immersive experience. Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path. The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; if the design does not support creation of this mental map, many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates. The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model. A mental model can be created by aiding the user to get, understand, or infer knowledge through the traditional methods of systematic study of a map of a place, exploration of real space, exploration of a copy of the real space or a model of the real space, or any combination of these methods.

E1732.name: odor
E1732.text: odor; also called: scent. Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama. A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor. For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research. When olfactory displays can generate odor effects, they are shown to induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and more immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness, also called cybersickness, to some extent.

E1745.text: user-centered software. The core design concern for user-centered software is designing usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.

E1746.name: interactive software
E1746.text: interactive software. The extended reality (XR) application software being developed is interactive software intended for laypersons, who may not know or need to know how the hardware or software works. In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

E1747.name: software engineering
E1747.text: software engineering. Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages.

E1748.name: design space
E1748.text: design space. A design space is the set of all possible designs, and when n distinct objects are placed on a screen without repetition, the typical size of the design space is n factorial, with the number of arrangements increasing if repetition is allowed. A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space.

E1749.name: calendar application
E1749.text: calendar application. A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space. In a calendar application, many possible designs may be invalid because dates must be ordered in a particular way, but in most practical systems a reasonably significant number of valid design choices can remain, such as 10, 15, or 20.

E1750.name: stage
E1750.text: stage. A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence. In interactive system design, users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants. A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage. In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

E1751.name: participant
E1751.text: participant; also called: participants. In interactive system design, users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants. An empirical study in interactive system development requires identifying participants, setting up the study, and obtaining participants' time. The empirical study was conducted with 34 participants: 20 male and 14 female, aged 15 to 47 years with a mean age of 29.3 years, and with heights of 159 to 170 centimeters with a mean height of 167.97 centimeters. Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

E1752.name: user-centric design approach
E1752.text: user-centric design approach. A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage.

E1753.name: iteration
E1753.text: iteration; also called: loop, iterations. The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin. The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly.

E1754.name: user feedback
E1754.text: user feedback; also called: feedback. In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

E1755.name: feasibility study
E1755.text: feasibility study; also called: feasibility study stage. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

E1756.name: requirement gathering
E1756.text: requirement gathering; also called: requirement gathering stage, usability requirement gathering. The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

E1757.name: analysis
E1757.text: analysis; also called: analysis of the data. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance. The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

E1758.name: specification
E1758.text: specification. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

E1759.name: design-prototype-evaluate cycle
E1759.text: design-prototype-evaluate cycle; also called: design-prototype-evaluate stage. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly. In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes. Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

E1760.name: design
E1760.text: design. In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

E1761.name: early evaluation
E1761.text: early evaluation. The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

E1762.name: code design
E1762.text: code design; also called: code-design. The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

E1763.name: implementation
E1763.text: implementation; also called: coding and implementation, overall implementation. Implementation in interactive system development involves coding followed by code testing; primary-level testing may be review-based, secondary-level testing may be more systematic or structured, such as black box or white box testing, and testing can be performed at unit levels, then integration, and then system-level testing.

E1764.name: code testing
E1764.text: code testing; also called: testing. Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing. In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test. The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study. Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view. The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

E1765.name: empirical study
E1765.text: empirical study; also called: empirical studies, usability study, study. The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study. The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing. The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved. An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects. An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

E1766.name: usability study
E1766.text: usability study. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

E1767.name: maintenance
E1767.text: maintenance. The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

E1768.name: end user
E1768.text: end user; also called: end users. In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes. In the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development, functional and non-functional requirements, including usability requirements, are collected from end users and clients, who may be the same but are usually different; usability requirements primarily come from end users, other non-functional requirements may come from clients, and functional requirements may come from both clients and end users.

E1769.name: requirement-gathering stage
E1769.text: requirement-gathering stage. In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

E1770.name: requirement analysis
E1770.text: requirement analysis. In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.

E1771.name: requirement
E1771.text: requirement; also called: requirements. A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

E1772.name: contextual inquiry
E1772.text: contextual inquiry; also called: CI, contextual inquiry methods. Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements. Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular. Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations. The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.

E1773.name: ethnographic study
E1773.text: ethnographic study; also called: ethnographic studies. Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

E1774.name: cultural probe
E1774.text: cultural probe; also called: cultural probes. Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

E1775.name: design-prototype-evaluate loop
E1775.text: design-prototype-evaluate loop. The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin. The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly. The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

E1776.name: turnaround time
E1776.text: turnaround time. The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly. Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, particularly the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, significantly affect a project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment. A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

E1777.name: interface design
E1777.text: interface design; also called: interface-design. The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

E1778.name: coding
E1778.text: coding; also called: code, coded. Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing. In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test. The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study. In the iterative design of usable extended reality systems, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops, such as the loop between requirement gathering and the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the loop between code design, coding, and code testing, and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent. Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, particularly the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, significantly affect a project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.

E1779.name: interactive system development
E1779.text: interactive system development; also called: interactive system development lifecycle, traditional interactive system development lifecycle, standard interactive system development lifecycle. Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing. The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing. The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved. Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users. In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable.

E1780.name: iterative software development life cycle
E1780.text: iterative software development life cycle. The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

E1781.name: executability
E1781.text: executability. Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

E1782.name: usability testing
E1782.text: usability testing; also called: usability-testing. The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing. A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it. The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing. Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable; usability testing or an empirical study is therefore needed to estimate usability, although usability was expected because the design-prototype-evaluate cycle was followed. In the traditional interactive system development lifecycle, deployment is reached only after all requirements are identified, coding is done, code is tested, and usability is tested; because each stage can take a long time, deployment may take a very long time.

E1783.name: iterative design
E1783.text: iterative design. In the iterative design of usable extended reality systems, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops, such as the loop between requirement gathering and the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the loop between code design, coding, and code testing, and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent.

E1785.name: development stage
E1785.text: development stage. When building usable extended reality systems, the development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

E1786.name: interactive system development lifecycle
E1786.text: interactive system development lifecycle; also called: ISDLC, interactive system development life cycles, interactive system development life cycle, ISDL. In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages. The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns. The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively. In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability. The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

E1788.text: system development lifecycle. Extended reality systems are examples of interactive systems, so the same system development lifecycle used for interactive systems can essentially be followed to build extended reality systems.

E1789.name: Majuli case study
E1789.text: Majuli case study. The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island. The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

E1790.name: digital preservation
E1790.text: digital preservation. Digital preservation is defined by UNESCO as the use of digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources.

E1791.name: evaluation
E1791.text: evaluation; also called: evaluation study. The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island. The evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour aims to measure usability aspects of the system, specifically user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment, and to identify potential areas for improvement by analyzing participants' responses and symptoms of cyber sickness. The evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour collected data from end users through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire, and participant responses were collected subjectively, objectively, or both. The structured questionnaire used in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation was related to the evaluation research question and could be used to measure objective data or behavioral data, or sometimes to collect data through a rating scale. In the evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour, the presence measure gave mostly good results, and prior experience may lead to even better results, with people with prior experience possibly finding the VR Tour more acceptable than people without prior experience.

E1792.name: Majuli River Island
E1792.text: Majuli River Island; also called: Majuli. Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender. Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius. Majuli's area was about 1250 square kilometers around 1900, had reduced to about 570 square kilometers in 1975, and had further reduced to about 427 square kilometers by 2021, with 2021 data giving about 427.09 square kilometers, an overall reduction of almost two-thirds and about a 25 percent reduction from 1975 to 2021. Majuli has been constantly hit by severe annual floods and erosion, and river erosion is consuming the island and reducing its habitable area, so formerly habitable areas are no longer habitable and have become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas. The severe annual floods and erosion of Majuli endanger its cultural resources and its material existence, and although measures are being taken to prevent further erosion, there is a real possibility that the island may disappear.

E1809.name: satra
E1809.text: satra; also called: Satras, sattras, Vaishnavite monasteries. Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts. Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes. Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total. Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest. The Majuli virtual tour contains a large number of geographically spread information points, including satras (Vaishnavite monasteries), villages, tribal villages, towns, and other places of interest, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.

In the standard interactive system development lifecycle, each stage requires a long time not only because of executing the stage but also because documentation for the stage must be prepared. Agile development is a development framework or approach that encourages fast development in practice, starts small by not trying to do everything from the beginning, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation, and ensures quick turnaround of projects that are more acceptable to clients. The agile development process flow consists of conceptualization, inception (creation of the team and arranging funds and resources), iteration or sprint (the development cycle, which includes all the other stages of the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC)), release (testing, training, and documentation, and deployment), production (ongoing support and maintenance), and retirement (end-of-life activities); conceptualization and inception together roughly refer to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering. An agile sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery: requirements are based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, then testing including training and documentation, then delivery to production.

The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them. In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen. The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

E1882.name: multimodal heritage archive
E1882.text: multimodal heritage archive. The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements. The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island captures tangible and intangible heritage aspects, including the indigenous architectural heritage of Satras and village life, cultural heritage, and ecological heritage such as the island's unique flora and fauna. In the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island, three-dimensional (3D) models were created from captured images to recreate the landscape, preserve ecological heritage, and recreate tangible architectural heritage. Two-dimensional (2D) drone shots and drone videos in the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island were used to showcase the landscape and top view of the locations and to digitally recreate and preserve cultural and ecological heritage, including the island's unique flora and fauna. The multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is used to recreate a more expansive virtual landscape and a virtual tour of the island.

E1883.name: 360-degree image

The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements. After processing a larger captured collection and keeping the minimum required material, the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island contains about 600 360-degree images, about 25 360-degree images per location, 5 360-degree videos, 11 two-dimensional (2D) regular videos capturing intangible cultural aspects, and 8 drone videos. In the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island, the high-definition 360-degree image resolution is 6720 by 3360, the drone 360-degree video resolution is 1920 by 960, and the drone video used for cultural and ecological preservation has resolution 3842 by 1920. The average file size in the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is 6.3 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree image, 100 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree video, 34 megabytes (MB) for a two-dimensional (2D) video used to capture cultural and intangible aspects, and 36 megabytes (MB) for a drone video. E1891.name: virtual space
E1891.text: virtual space. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was created by recreating Majuli island in virtual space from archival information, with the objective of providing an immersive interactive experience of the island's tangible and intangible heritage. Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone. The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

E1892.text: user requirement; also called: requirements, user requirements. The key challenges in building the interactive Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour are understanding the users, understanding their requirements, and converting those requirements into design ideas that can be implemented. A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it. Designing an immersive experience involves the design-prototype-evaluation cycle in order to incorporate user requirements.

E1898.text: system-centered design; also called: SCD. E1906.name: functional requirement
E1906.text: functional requirement; also called: FR, functional requirements. Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements are the system features and abilities to carry out tasks, expressed as functions treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input once implemented. The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements. Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier. A functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that is easy to convert into code because it specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output, and an optional description of its purpose.

E1907.name: non-functional requirement
E1907.text: non-functional requirement; also called: NFR, non-functional requirements. Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements. Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions and are typically related to quality attributes of software. Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable. Categories of non-functional requirements include performance-related requirements, operating constraints, economic considerations, lifecycle requirements, and interface issues.

E1917.name: phenomenological research method
E1917.text: phenomenological research method. Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular.

E1918.name: semi-structured interview
E1918.text: semi-structured interview; also called: semi-structured interview process. Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.

E1919.name: interview
E1919.text: interview; also called: interviews, interviewing people. Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations. The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities. Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes. Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices.

E1920.name: observation
names: observing people in their natural work settings
E1920.text: observation; also called: observations, observing people in their natural work settings. Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations. The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities. Observations and interaction with users in contextual inquiry enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace, which supports design decisions. The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure. The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.

E1921.name: user behavior
E1921.text: user behavior. Knowing how users behave in a specific work context is essential to ensure that the software, product, or system being built is usable, because usability is defined with respect to that specific work context. The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.

E1927.text: system development. Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting, reveals their unique behavioral traits, and enables design refinement; without it, designers may create invalid designs and give essential user activities equal importance to unnecessary features, compromising usability.

User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group.

E1930.name: calendar app
E1930.text: calendar app. User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group. In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting. In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

E1932.name: active mode
E1932.text: active mode. Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

E1934.name: master-apprentice model
E1934.text: master-apprentice model. In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.

E1935.name: plan stage
E1935.text: plan stage; also called: plan. The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process. The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.

E1937.name: execute stage
E1937.text: execute stage; also called: execute. The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process. The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data. The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

E1938.name: close stage
E1938.text: close stage; also called: close. The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process. The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.

E1939.name: reflect stage
E1939.text: reflect stage; also called: reflect. The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process. The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals. The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.

E1941.name: affinity diagram method
E1941.text: affinity diagram method; also called: affinity diagram, affinity-diagram. The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals. The affinity diagram method is a method for analyzing data collected through contextual inquiry, and it consists of five steps: generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a header or name for each group, and draw the finished diagram. In the affinity diagram method, the generated ideas are the observers' final notes from contextual inquiry, possibly refined in later processing, and displaying the ideas means putting those notes together in a place such as a wall or a board. Sorting ideas into groups in the affinity diagram method is done to find patterns among ideas that may look random, by moving similar ideas into the same group so that meaningful conclusions can be drawn. In the affinity diagram method, a group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group after the ideas have been sorted, and it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas within that group; the header is not present in the initial ideas.

E1942.name: design specification

Design recommendations or guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices that do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account. E1956.name: function

E1967.name: Majuli virtual reality tour
E1967.text: Majuli virtual reality tour; also called: VR Tour. Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour is intended for people who do not reside on Majuli rather than residents, because residents are least likely to use it since they are already on the island. Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices. The usability of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour is claimed only for the three identified user groups—students or learners, tourists, and pilgrims—and it is not claimed to be usable for any person in any work context or task. Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

E1968.name: virtual reality tour
E1968.text: virtual reality tour; also called: VR tour, system-controlled virtual reality tour, virtual tour. Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques. Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements. System-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to concentrate more on the experience itself. Lack of user involvement in system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement. The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

E1974.name: design challenge
E1974.text: design challenge; also called: key design challenge. A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness. A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide both tangible and intangible heritage experiences and to combine them for a seamless user experience. Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

E1975.name: large geographical area
E1975.text: large geographical area; also called: large geography, large geographies, large space. A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness. The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does. Accurate location information in any virtual reality (VR) tour is crucial, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space. Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

E1977.name: data subset restriction
E1977.text: data subset restriction; also called: data-subset restriction, subset of the collected data. The data-subset restriction in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail, reduced the possibility of cyber sickness, and increased interest for each group, whereas making the entire data set accessible to all users could confuse users, reduce their interest, and lead to cyber sickness.

Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language. Interface and interaction design requires creativity and imagination, and the design process can be started from creativity aided by intuition, expertise, experience, or domain knowledge, and/or from guidelines, often called checklists, heuristics, or thumb rules. E2000.text: Shneiderman's first golden rule. Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design is to strive for consistency. The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

E2002.name: internal consistency
E2002.text: internal consistency. The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency. Internal consistency in system design means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than using separate objects, elements, or interactions.

E2003.name: external consistency
E2003.text: external consistency; also called: environmental consistency. The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency. External or environmental consistency in system design means that the elements and interactions in a virtual world should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge, so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world as closely as possible.

E2004.name: Shneiderman's second golden rule
E2004.text: Shneiderman's second golden rule. Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

E2005.name: universal usability
E2005.text: universal usability. Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

E2006.text: menu-based option; also called: menu options. Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

E2011.text: usable design. The third rule of usable design is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action the user performs.

E2012.name: informative feedback
E2012.text: informative feedback. The third rule of usable design is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action the user performs. A progress bar is informative feedback that sometimes appears during a task, shows the percentage of the task completed, and gives the user a sense of how much longer to wait; without it, the user cannot tell what the system is doing or how much of the task is completed. A color change on a save icon after a save operation is informative feedback that indicates the save operation is done successfully; without it, the user cannot tell whether the save operation worked.

E2017.name: error prevention
E2017.text: error prevention. The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling. In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action. Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

E2018.name: error handling
E2018.text: error handling; also called: simple error handling. The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling. In system design, when an error occurs, error handling should give simple, easy-to-understand information rather than complicated error messages, because complicated messages can confuse and scare the user.

E2025.name: usability rule
E2025.text: usability rule; also called: generic usability rules. The last usability rule, reducing short-term memory load, requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks for the user's optimum outcome, and not forcing users to remember more than nine chunks. The eight generic usability rules are not specific to a particular product or system, and they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

E2027.name: human memory
E2027.text: human memory. In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

E2028.name: short-term memory
E2028.text: short-term memory. In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities. George Miller's 1956 psychological finding, the seven plus or minus two rule, gives the short-term memory limit as five to nine chunks of information at a time, so holding fewer underutilizes short-term memory and holding more overutilizes it and is harmful.

E2034.name: object interaction
E2034.text: object interaction; also called: object manipulation. Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings. In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation. In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint. Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

E2036.name: interaction for system control

Interaction for system control is an interaction technique whose goal is to issue commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file, and these commands are most of the regular operations associated with using any software. Interactive methods for system control include physical controllers such as buttons and switches; graphical menus, adapted two-dimensional (2D) menus suitable for three-dimensional (3D) massive environments, one degree of freedom menus, and three-dimensional widgets; voice commands; gesture commands such as mimic gestures, symbolic gestures, sweeping gestures, sign language, speech-corrected hand gestures, and whole-body interactions; tools such as physical tools, virtual tools, and tangible interfaces; and multimodal interaction techniques that combine multiple techniques, for example voice with gestures or other interactions.

E2041.name: object selection technique
E2041.text: object selection technique; also called: selection technique. For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized. Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection. The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection. Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.
