E2049.name: pointing-based selection
E2049.text: pointing-based selection. Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller. Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. A virtual ray in pointing-based selection is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable. Some pointing-based selection methods combine gaze pointing to estimate the target and hand pointing to trigger selection. Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

E2050.name: image plane selection
E2050.text: image plane selection; also called: occlusion, framing. The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection. Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance. In image plane selection, the user holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the desired object and provides a signal, such as a gesture or hand movement, to select the object when it lines up with the hand and the eye. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common. Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.

E2053.name: hand selection technique
E2053.text: hand selection technique. A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand. Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection. The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements. The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly. Intent-driven selection is a hand selection technique in which the user moves the virtual hand toward an object and positions virtual fingers, or uses the posture of virtual fingers, around the object to indicate the user's level of confidence in selecting that object.

E2054.name: grab

E2055.name: virtual hand technique
E2055.text: virtual hand technique; also called: virtual hand. Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection. The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements. The virtual hand technique has a problem for selecting distant objects because moving the physical hand to reach them can require a long duration of physical hand movement, which can be tiring and annoying.

E2056.name: go-go technique
E2056.text: go-go technique; also called: go-go. Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection. The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly. The go-go technique has a low-precision problem for selecting distant small objects because the virtual hand moves faster when the object is farther away, so a small physical hand movement can miss, bypass, or cross the target and is difficult to control. For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go. In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

E2057.name: prism technique
E2057.text: prism technique; also called: prism. Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection. The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still. For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go. Prism can result in a mismatch between the real and virtual hand positions because it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive. In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

E2072.name: ray casting
E2072.text: ray casting; also called: ray casting technique. Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray. In ray casting, selecting small distant objects is difficult and can require practice because the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when the small object is surrounded by other objects of similar, smaller, or larger size. Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending. Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker. Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.

E2073.name: bend cast
E2073.text: bend cast. Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending. Bend cast works best when only a few objects are near the ray's path, because with many nearby objects and similar distances the intended object may not be the closest, reintroducing the precision problem.

E2078.name: two-dimensional
E2078.text: two-dimensional; also called: 2D. Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance. In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane. In the framing hands technique, the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in the two-dimensional (2D) image surrounding an object, as typically seen while capturing movies or such visual media. Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

E2079.name: view plane
E2079.text: view plane; also called: clipping window, 2D view plane. Projection transformation maps objects described in a three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane. The view plane used in projection is usually a rectangular area, also called a clipping window. A view volume is a three-dimensional (3D) region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is projected onto the view plane, so objects inside the view volume are projected and objects outside it are discarded. Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated. Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet.

E2080.name: head crusher technique
E2080.text: head crusher technique. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common. In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane.

E2081.name: image plane
E2081.text: image plane. In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane. In the framing hands technique, the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in the two-dimensional (2D) image surrounding an object, as typically seen while capturing movies or such visual media.

E2082.name: sticky finger technique
E2082.text: sticky finger technique. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common. In the sticky finger technique, the object underneath the user's finger is selected.

E2083.name: lifting palm technique
E2083.text: lifting palm technique. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common. In the lifting palm technique, the user selects an object by flattening the outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the desired object as if trying to lift the object with the palm.

E2084.name: framing hands technique
E2084.text: framing hands technique; also called: framing hands. The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common. In the framing hands technique, the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in the two-dimensional (2D) image surrounding an object, as typically seen while capturing movies or such visual media.

E2085.name: volumetric selection
E2085.text: volumetric selection. The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection. Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone. The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting the objects within the cone. The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique in which a sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface and the objects found within the sphere are selected. Volumetric selection techniques are most useful for selecting small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment, and selecting smaller objects becomes problematic with any volumetric selection technique when the virtual environment is complex with many objects.

E2086.name: box
E2086.text: box. Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone. The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

E2089.text: cone casting flashlight technique. The cone casting flashlight technique can select multiple objects because the cone is volumetric, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects may be difficult.

E2094.name: object manipulation
E2094.text: object manipulation; also called: manipulation. Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object. Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

E2095.name: scale
E2095.text: scale. Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object. The transform property attached to every game object in a scene stores the object's position, rotation, and scale, and it can be modified programmatically through a script, for example in the update function by using transform.Translate, rotation values, and local scale values, to make the object behave as desired.

E2096.name: texture
E2096.text: texture; also called: textures, texture images, stored texture images. A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data. In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape. In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

E2097.name: behavior
E2097.text: behavior. Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

E2098.name: manipulation technique
E2098.text: manipulation technique; also called: manipulation techniques. Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

E2099.name: hand manipulation
E2099.text: hand manipulation. Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation. Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea and uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects. Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects. Hand manipulation requires somewhat more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly.

E2100.name: indirect manipulation
E2100.text: indirect manipulation. Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object. Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object. Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

E2106.name: three-dimensional widget
E2106.text: three-dimensional widget; also called: 3D widget, three-dimensional widgets. Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object. Each three-dimensional (3D) widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of a given object; instead, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using the individual widgets.

E2107.name: indirect proxy
E2107.text: indirect proxy. Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world. World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

E2108.text: local proxy. E2111.name: world in miniature
E2111.text: world in miniature; also called: WIM. World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world. World in miniature (WIM) allows manipulation of virtual objects both within and outside the user's reach; for a distant object, the user does not need to select it, but can manipulate its representation in the miniature model, which then manipulates the distant object. Implementing world in miniature (WIM) for large and complex virtual environments is not very practical because creating the miniature model for such environments is very difficult.

E2112.name: miniature model
E2112.text: miniature model. E2113.name: bimanual manipulation technique
E2113.text: bimanual manipulation technique. A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously. The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

E2114.name: synchronous
E2114.text: synchronous; also called: synchronous hand movement. A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously. The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle. The spindle technique is not easy to use because it requires synchronous hand movement while interacting in a virtual world, which is not necessarily easy for everybody and requires a lot of practice to use efficiently. Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique and an extension of the spindle technique, in which both hands need to be moved together but need not be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

E2115.name: asynchronous
E2115.text: asynchronous. A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

E2116.name: spindle technique
E2116.text: spindle technique; also called: spindle. The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle. In the spindle technique, moving both hands in unison can move a virtual world object, and the technique can also be used to rotate the object simultaneously. The spindle technique is not easy to use because it requires synchronous hand movement while interacting in a virtual world, which is not necessarily easy for everybody and requires a lot of practice to use efficiently. Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique and an extension of the spindle technique, in which both hands need to be moved together but need not be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

E2121.name: integrated hybrid manipulation technique
E2121.text: integrated hybrid manipulation technique. Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques are techniques that switch automatically from selection to manipulation after selection, without any explicit signal from the user, and switch back to selection mode after manipulation. Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.

E2122.name: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting
names: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting
E2122.text: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting; also called: HOMER. Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately. In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), the user selects an object using a ray casting technique, and when the ray intersects the desired object, the user's virtual hand moves automatically to the object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object. In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), after the user's virtual hand attaches to the object, the technique switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation. In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), manipulation ends when the user indicates to the system that the manipulation job is done through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.

E2123.name: system control interaction
E2123.text: system control interaction. System control interaction is a third category of interaction that primarily relies on regular interaction techniques that are familiar when dealing with any computer system.

E2124.name: travel
E2124.text: travel; also called: travel part. The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.

E2125.name: wayfinding
E2125.text: wayfinding; also called: wayfinding part. Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding. Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world. Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path. For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively. Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

E2126.name: exploration
E2126.text: exploration. Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

E2127.name: search
E2127.text: search. E2129.name: walking-based locomotion
E2129.text: walking-based locomotion. Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment. Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

E2130.name: selection-based locomotion
E2130.text: selection-based locomotion. Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking. Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion. Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

E2131.name: manipulation-based locomotion
E2131.text: manipulation-based locomotion. Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion. In the four broad locomotion technique types, object manipulation may not be involved in walking-based, steering-based, or selection-based locomotion; manipulation-based locomotion involves navigating by manipulating certain things, and navigation mostly involves no object manipulation while manipulation is not entirely avoided when implementing travel techniques in an immersive setting. Manipulation-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world. Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.

E2132.name: full gait technique
E2132.text: full gait technique. Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques. In full gait techniques, the user actually walks in the real world and that walk is translated to virtual movement in a virtual environment, which is the most natural way to travel. In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation, so walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.

E2133.name: partial gait technique
E2133.text: partial gait technique. Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques. In a partial gait technique, the user walks in place, so the user does not change position and is not actually moving forward, backward, left, or right. Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

E2134.name: gait negation technique
E2134.text: gait negation technique. Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques. Gait negation techniques require a specialized setup that cancels the user's lateral movements and keeps the user's physical position fixed, because natural walking involves lateral movement that may be difficult to map to a focused virtual movement, and the setup detects and eliminates the lateral movement before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation, making it easier for the system to understand the user's intention. Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

E2144.name: steering-based navigation
E2144.text: steering-based navigation. Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another, and continuous control of direction and speed essentially indicates that a system has implemented steering-based navigation. Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware.

E2145.name: spatial steering-based navigation
E2145.text: spatial steering-based navigation. Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware. Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, where looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking; hand-directed, where hand gestures determine the direction of travel; or body-leaning directed, where leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

E2146.name: physical steering-based navigation
E2146.text: physical steering-based navigation. Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware. Physical steering-based navigation involves physical setups or separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms and virtual reality (VR) simulators for aircraft, merchant ships, cars, boats and spaceships, in which physically moving the steering controls travel in the virtual world.

E2152.name: target selection-based locomotion
E2152.text: target selection-based locomotion. Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion. In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to the target. Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world. Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path. The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model. Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points. Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

E2161.name: destination
E2161.text: destination; also called: desired destination. Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world. Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination. Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time. The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves. The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

E2199.name: user experience design
E2199.text: user experience design. The design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was framed by its broader objectives of capturing tangible and intangible heritage, enhancing user presence, and minimizing cyber sickness, with corresponding design considerations of user experience design, exploration of the island, and handling cyber sickness. In user experience design, the first stage is to identify the users, so that the experience can be designed accordingly.

E2200.name: minimap
E2200.text: minimap; also called: local minimap, overall island minimap. A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place. On the minimap, white dots represent the arrangement of the 360-degree images; the user navigates by moving from one image to another along the dots, and the arrangement provides direction and orientation; the user's current image is highlighted green. For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support. The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

E2201.name: notification system
E2201.text: notification system. User feedback and interaction with users for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour led to incorporated design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

E2203.name: user categories
E2203.text: user categories; also called: user category. Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

E2204.name: information point
E2204.text: information point. The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration. The Majuli virtual tour contains a large number of geographically spread information points, including satras (Vaishnavite monasteries), villages, tribal villages, towns, and other places of interest, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.

The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

E2211.name: preprocessing
E2211.text: preprocessing. Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

E2212.name: quality of experience
E2212.text: quality of experience. Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow. In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception. In computer graphics, lighting models and shading models are distinct, although they may physically represent more or less similar things, and they are differentiated by the computation involved: lighting models involve more computation than shading models, and shading models are used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience. If aliasing is left unaddressed, it may lead to distortion that is visible with a change in resolution and that will reduce the quality of experience.

E2215.text: image editing tool. The images and videos, mostly the images, were edited with image editing tools for uniform illumination because the 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another will make the user feel that something is odd.

E2216.name: ambient sound
E2216.text: ambient sound. Ambient sounds such as temple bells, birds chirping, and bike horns were added and played depending on the place being visited to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience, with temple bells played for a satra or a religious site. The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound.

E2217.name: virtual tablet interface
E2217.text: virtual tablet interface. The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content. The navigation tools of the virtual tablet interface include a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map. The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place. The virtual tablet interface provides access to information content through info elements. The design of the virtual tablet interface is inspired by real-world tablet use so that it is familiar and easy for users to use.

E2227.text: arrow. An arrow shown to the user indicates a direction, and selecting the arrow moves the user in that direction along the arrangement of the 360-degree images.

E2228.name: notification
E2228.text: notification; also called: notifications. At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

E2229.name: cultural video
E2229.text: cultural video; also called: cultural videos. At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface. The Oculus Quest version of the Majuli VR Tour used 597 images, 11 cultural videos, 8 drone videos, and 5 360-degree videos, while the Google Cardboard mobile version used all 597 images in compressed form, no cultural videos, no drone videos, and 1 360-degree video for the initial experience. The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound. At different points in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, cultural videos and activities are available, and a notification for cultural videos is played on the tablet interface. To optimize size in the mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, most videos and cultural videos are omitted, and only some prominent videos are used.

E2230.name: information icon
E2230.text: information icon. At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface. In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

E2231.name: tablet interface
E2231.text: tablet interface. In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos. The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type.

E2232.name: dual maps
E2232.text: dual maps. For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

E2233.name: local interface
E2233.text: local interface. For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

E2234.name: orientation awareness
E2234.text: orientation awareness. The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

E2235.name: mental map
E2235.text: mental map. The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind. Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

E2236.name: island tour
E2236.text: island tour. In the island tour, each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

E2237.name: view interpolation
E2237.text: view interpolation. View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause and that reduce the user experience.

E2238.name: navigation arrow
E2238.text: navigation arrow. Navigation arrows guide the user from one image to another, prevent random movement, and create a seamless exploration experience while supporting smooth travel.

E2239.name: virtual vehicle metaphor
E2239.text: virtual vehicle metaphor. A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.

E2240.name: walking-based navigation
E2240.text: walking-based navigation. Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required.

E2241.name: virtual vehicle travel technique
E2241.text: virtual vehicle travel technique. The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves. The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

E2242.name: seated viewpoint
E2242.text: seated viewpoint. E2244.name: route
E2244.text: route. Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

E2248.name: virtual tour system
E2248.text: virtual tour system. In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos. The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type. The virtual tour system provides textual descriptions of a place as informative notifications and descriptions that provide additional context about locations and significant spots. In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

Inside a location in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user can move forward and backward using arrow keys and can see icons intended to provide information.

E2251.name: point of interest
E2251.text: point of interest; also called: significant spot, POIs, points of interest, POI. The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest. A point of interest (POI) in the Satra graph does not have to refer to an actual physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are. When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior. The maximum wait time at a point of interest (POI) is the time a user needs to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation. Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

E2252.text: point-of-interest awareness. E2254.name: controlled navigation technique
E2254.text: controlled navigation technique; also called: controlled navigation. The system design implemented a controlled navigation technique to minimize cybersickness, in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort and reduces the chances of discomfort.

E2257.text: visual cue; also called: visual cues. E2261.name: usability evaluation
E2261.text: usability evaluation; also called: empirical evaluation, empirical study, empirical usability evaluation, quick usability evaluation technique, quick evaluation method. In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly. Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

E2262.name: analysis and specification
E2262.text: analysis and specification. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

E2263.name: quick evaluation
E2263.text: quick evaluation. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly. In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes. Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering. In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent. The interface design part of interactive system development uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping, and quick evaluation of the prototype; design may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, quick evaluation may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the cycle is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

E2264.name: coding and implementation
E2264.text: coding and implementation; also called: implementation. The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly. Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation in interactive system development are standard software development lifecycle (SDLC) stages with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality system design or implementation. E2268.name: experience design
E2268.text: experience design. The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

E2269.name: cost overrun
E2269.text: cost overrun. A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

E2270.name: prototyping techniques
E2270.text: prototyping techniques. Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

E2271.name: full implementation
E2271.text: full implementation. A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first. A full implementation of a software idea involves highly skilled manpower, specifically programmers, and many cost components, including setting up or procuring resources and engaging the manpower, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted.

E2272.name: final product
E2272.text: final product. A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

E2273.name: horizontal prototype
E2273.text: horizontal prototype; also called: horizontal prototypes. Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes. A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it. Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable. In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype. Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

E2274.name: vertical prototype
E2274.text: vertical prototype; also called: vertical prototypes. Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes. A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system. Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions. In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment. In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

E2275.name: functionality
E2275.text: functionality. A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it. A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.

E2276.name: system
E2276.text: system. A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system. Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users. In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable. To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

E2277.name: low-fidelity prototype
E2277.text: low-fidelity prototype. A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example. To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

E2278.name: low-fidelity prototyping
E2278.text: low-fidelity prototyping; also called: low-fidelity prototyping approach. Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes compared with approaches that require coding and computers, and it is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability. Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes. To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction. A medium-fidelity prototyping approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes without involving coding, whereas a low-fidelity prototyping approach does not rely on computers or digital media. High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

E2279.name: horizontal prototyping
E2279.text: horizontal prototyping. Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.

E2280.name: interface sketch
E2280.text: interface sketch; also called: sketch, single interface sketch. An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned. A single interface sketch is primarily used to represent a horizontal prototype and is not sufficient to prototype interactions because it does not show the sequence of user actions and the corresponding interface changes needed to execute a task. To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction. In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end. The overall purpose of a prototype is to convert an idea into a prototype, evaluate it, and revise the idea and prototype if evaluation finds issues; consequently, an interface sketch need not be replicated exactly in the final design, and feedback can change interface elements, their appearance, position, or layout.

A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

E2293.name: wizard of oz approach
E2293.text: wizard of oz approach; also called: wizard of oz setup. The Wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator, called the wizard, operates the computer and returns the requested response or result to the subject. International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available. The 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup consisted of a human user speaking into a microphone while facing a computer that the user believed was a real computer, a hidden wizard separated from the user by a wall, and two computers connected through an intermediary. The hidden wizard in the 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup heard the user's speech through the microphone that was also connected to a computer speaker, typed the corresponding characters, and the characters were transmitted to the user's screen, making the user believe that the speech had been automatically converted, although no automatic technology existed at that time to convert the speech into the displayed text.

names: listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup
E2296.text: listening typewriter experiment; also called: listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup. International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available. The 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup consisted of a human user speaking into a microphone while facing a computer that the user believed was a real computer, a hidden wizard separated from the user by a wall, and two computers connected through an intermediary. The hidden wizard in the 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup heard the user's speech through the microphone that was also connected to a computer speaker, typed the corresponding characters, and the characters were transmitted to the user's screen, making the user believe that the speech had been automatically converted, although no automatic technology existed at that time to convert the speech into the displayed text.

E2298.name: throwaway prototype
E2298.text: throwaway prototype. Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes. Throwaway prototypes are prototypes that are used for quick evaluation and then discarded. Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

E2299.name: incremental prototype
E2299.text: incremental prototype. Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes. Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.

E2300.name: evolutionary prototype
E2300.text: evolutionary prototype. Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes. Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results until it becomes the final product, rather than prototyping separate modules and combining them.

E2304.name: expert evaluation
E2304.text: expert evaluation; also called: quick evaluation of prototypes, quick evaluation, quick or expert evaluation. Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup. The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators. Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users. Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users. The evaluation team for expert evaluation should have at least three to five members; more members are welcome, but three to five is sufficient.

The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators. In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues. Heuristic evaluation requires a team of at least three to five evaluators, who can be members of design teams or other skilled or expert designers not necessarily involved in the design team. E2316.name: cognitive walkthrough
E2316.text: cognitive walkthrough. Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype. A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost. A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard. In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype. Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.

E2317.name: usability inspection

E2318.name: usability problem
E2318.text: usability problem; also called: usability issue, usability problems. Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype. Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks. The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues. Nielsen's 10 heuristics can be used to identify usability problems at an early stage of design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional in heuristic evaluation, unlike the cognitive walkthrough method, where a vertical prototype is mandatory. The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.

E2336.name: Nielsen's ten heuristics
E2336.text: Nielsen's ten heuristics; also called: Nielsen's 10 heuristics. Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems. Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support. Nielsen's 10 heuristics can be used to identify usability problems at an early stage of design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional in heuristic evaluation, unlike the cognitive walkthrough method, where a vertical prototype is mandatory.
