E2346.name: user evaluation
E2346.text: user evaluation; also called: evaluation with self-reports. User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional. User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data. In user evaluation, collecting user feedback with rating scales is easy compared with more rigorous evaluation techniques. In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions. One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging.

E2347.name: subjective data
E2347.text: subjective data. User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

E2348.name: preference data
E2348.text: preference data. User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

E2349.name: questionnaire
E2349.text: questionnaire; also called: questionnaires. In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions. One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging. In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session. Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003. Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

E2350.text: post-task data collection. Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.

E2351.name: after scenario questionnaire
E2351.text: after scenario questionnaire; also called: ASQ. The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'. In the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), users rate each statement on a seven-point rating scale in which rating 1 means strongly disagree with the statement and rating 7 means strongly agree with the statement. The three statements of the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be roughly mapped to the three usability measures in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) definition: ease of completing the tasks relates to effectiveness, the amount of time taken to complete the tasks relates to efficiency, and the three statements together represent satisfaction. Feedback from the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be summarised by taking either the average rating for each statement across all users who participated in the evaluation or the average rating for all statements taken together.

E2354.name: system usability scale
E2354.text: system usability scale; also called: SUS. The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks. The System Usability Scale (SUS) consists of 10 numbered statements: 1, 'I think that I would like to use this system frequently' (positive); 2, 'I found the system unnecessarily complex' (negative); 3, 'I thought the system was easy to use' (positive); 4, 'I think I would need the support of a technical person to be able to use the system' (negative); 5, 'I found the various functions in this system were well integrated' (positive); 6, 'I thought the system was too inconsistent' (negative); 7, 'I would imagine that most people would learn to use the system very quickly' (positive); 8, 'I found the system very cumbersome to use' (negative); 9, 'I felt very confident using the system' (positive); and 10, 'I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system' (negative); each even-numbered statement is the negatively worded counterpart of the preceding odd-numbered statement. Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree. The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ_{i∈{1,3,5,7,9}}(r_i − 1) + Σ_{i∈{2,4,6,8,10}}(5 − r_i)), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i. The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.

E2366.text: expert evaluation technique; also called: expert evaluation techniques. The interface design part of interactive system development uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping, and quick evaluation of the prototype; design may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, quick evaluation may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the cycle is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues. Code design in interactive system development requires producing a code design through iterations and brainstorming, using design languages or notations such as data flow diagram (DFD), entity relationship (ER), object-oriented approaches, and unified modeling language (UML). To deliver within an agile sprint, the development team holds daily meetings or brainstorming, provides a live demonstration after each iteration, and regularly collects quick feedback from stakeholders and customers, which is shared with the team before the next sprint so that it can be addressed; this keeps the team agile by making changes based on feedback as quickly as possible.

E2370.name: Majuli VR Tour
E2370.text: Majuli VR Tour. The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions. The Majuli VR Tour used the Extended Reality (XR) toolkit for its Oculus Quest version and the Google Virtual Reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) for its Google Cardboard version. Autodesk Maya software was used to create the three-dimensional (3D) models for the Majuli VR Tour immersive experience, using real images as references and as textures on the modeled objects. The initial Majuli VR Tour application size was 9.85 gigabytes (GB) because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread. To reduce the space requirements of the Majuli VR Tour, all videos were stored in cloud services and loaded from the cloud when a user clicked a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest video player, so the videos were not always stored on the client device, reducing the application size to 5.1 gigabytes (GB).

E2371.text: Unity engine. A Unity C-sharp (C#) script file begins with a namespace component, with using statements such as using Unity engine and using system.collections, and defines a public class, typically inherited from MonoBehaviour, whose name is the same as the file name.

E2372.name: Oculus Quest 2
E2372.text: Oculus Quest 2; also called: Oculus Quest. The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, and does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer. Compared with a high-end graphics workstation, the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage, so the Oculus Quest 2 application required optimization to reduce its size and associated computations, including memory access, because reducing the size reduces rendering requirements and the associated memory access. The Oculus Quest 2 application used a cloud computing-based optimization in which all videos, not images, were stored in the cloud because videos take up more space; when a user selected a video thumbnail from the Oculus Quest 2 video player, the video was loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally, reducing storage and data-access requirements. Because the videos were stored in the cloud, the application deployed on the Oculus Quest 2 client device was reduced to 5.1 gigabytes (GB), and a corresponding computational reduction occurred. The cloud-based video-loading optimization for the Oculus Quest 2 application relied on a cloud server, so it required high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time; if these network connectivity issues were not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.

E2380.text: video playback; also called: video playback support. The optimization strategy for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli virtual reality system was to compress the images to reduce storage requirements and to remove video playback support, because most videos could not be utilized. Compressing the images and removing video playback support made the Majuli virtual reality system experience less realistic than the full version implementation. Compressing the images and removing video playback support reduced the overall size of the Majuli virtual reality system from roughly 10 gigabytes (GB) to 0.7 gigabytes. Approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences include cloud-based services, which could allow video playback to be retained, and compression techniques, while in extreme cases some features may have to be removed.

E2381.name: Oculus Quest
E2381.text: Oculus Quest; also called: Oculus Quest headset. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard. The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound. The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses three-dimensional (3D) models to create the experience instead of 360-degree images and videos. The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience, with simpler controls and fewer features, but its navigation, selection, and manipulation modes are more or less the same.

E2382.name: 360-degree image tour
E2382.text: 360-degree image tour; also called: 360-degree-image tour, 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality tour implementation. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard. The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound. In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system. After user group selection in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user experiences a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island, using a 360-degree video captured during field trips. When the user reaches the riverbank in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, a tablet interface appears that lets the user select a location on a map and move to that particular location.

E2383.name: three-dimensional model tour
names: three-dimensional model Majuli virtual reality tour implementation
E2383.text: three-dimensional model tour; also called: 3D model tour, three-dimensional model Majuli virtual reality tour implementation. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard. The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses three-dimensional (3D) models to create the experience instead of 360-degree images and videos. The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation includes models of the entrance to Kamalabadi Satra, the entire campus with roads, and the villages and dwelling units. The three-dimensional (3D) models in the model-based Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation use textures from real images to create a realistic-looking appearance.

E2384.name: mobile-device tour
names: mobile-device Majuli virtual reality tour implementation
E2384.text: mobile-device tour; also called: mobile-device Majuli virtual reality tour implementation. The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard. The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for Google Cardboard, in which the user's smartphone is inserted into the Google Cardboard device to provide a 360-degree experience. The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience, with simpler controls and fewer features, but its navigation, selection, and manipulation modes are more or less the same. To optimize size in the mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, most videos and cultural videos are omitted, and only some prominent videos are used. The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation retains the boat-ride experience and a tablet interface in a different form, with a minimap available at each place.

E2390.text: vehicle-metaphor route-planning method. E2391.name: empirical evaluation
E2391.text: empirical evaluation; also called: empirical study, usability study, empirical research, usability research, empirical research process. Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users. In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable. Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, empirical research, or usability research, means observation in the real world of real users. Empirical evaluation is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability of the system. The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

E2392.name: quick prototype evaluation
E2392.text: quick prototype evaluation. Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

E2393.name: usability assessment
E2393.text: usability assessment; also called: usability evaluation. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data. A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

E2394.name: fully implemented system
E2394.text: fully implemented system. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

E2395.name: controlled experiment
E2395.text: controlled experiment; also called: empirical research, empirical study, user study, usability study, controlled empirical experiment, standard controlled experiment. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data. A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

E2396.name: user behavioral data
E2396.text: user behavioral data. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

E2397.name: research question
E2397.text: research question; also called: RQ2, RQ3. An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects. The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question. The research question 'Is the new text entry graphical user interface (GUI) good?' is problematic because asking several users, for example five users, to judge its quality can produce divided judgments, such as two good, two poor or very bad, and one in between, neither good nor bad, so no answer to the question is likely and no conclusion can be drawn. Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users. Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

E2398.name: variable
E2398.text: variable; also called: variables. An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects. The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables. In the variables stage of empirical research, the variables in the testable questions are identified to design an experiment; the two most important variable types are independent variables, or factors, which can take levels or values, and dependent variables, which depend on the factors and levels.

E2399.name: experiment
E2399.text: experiment. An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

E2400.name: data
E2400.text: data. An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

E2401.name: empirical data
E2401.text: empirical data; also called: experimental data. An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface. The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question. In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed. A straightforward conclusion from experimental data can be misleading because an observed result may be due to chance, and if it is due to chance, changing the participants or conditions may produce different data and a different conclusion. The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

E2451.name: within-subject design
E2451.text: within-subject design; also called: repeated measures design. In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants. Within-subject designs are easier to manage than between-subject designs, but choosing between them depends on circumstances, such as the availability of participants and resources, which may force a between-subject design. In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface. To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied; statistically, these random or systematic variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.

E2469.name: experimental design
E2469.text: experimental design; also called: design of the experiment. The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data. For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design. For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test. For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels. For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

E2474.text: paired sample t-test. E2492.name: case study

E2493.name: user engagement

E2498.name: standard deviation
E2498.text: standard deviation. The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16). E2527.name: Majuli virtual tour
E2527.text: Majuli virtual tour; also called: Majuli virtual tour system. The cyber sickness evaluation of the Majuli virtual tour used the SSQ questionnaire and collected pre-exposure and post-exposure data for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor effects, and total severity. The box plots of average pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour system did not generally induce cyber sickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference. The statistical significance test performed on the pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour was a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and it revealed a statistically significant difference between pre- and post-exposure outcomes for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item. The statistically significant pre- to post-exposure change in total sickness in the Majuli virtual tour indicates that the Majuli virtual tour design had some effect on total sickness.

The box plots of average pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour system did not generally induce cyber sickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference. Box plots of the realism and preference ratings showed that instantaneous speed produced higher realism ratings and higher user preference than constant speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed these differences were statistically significant.

E2550.name: agile development
E2550.text: agile development. Agile development is a development framework or approach that encourages fast development in practice, starts small by not trying to do everything from the beginning, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation, and ensures quick turnaround of projects that are more acceptable to clients. Agile development keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, unlike the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) method, where the system is first completed and then delivered. The agile development process flow consists of conceptualization, inception (creation of the team and arranging funds and resources), iteration or sprint (the development cycle, which includes all the other stages of the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC)), release (testing, training, and documentation, and deployment), production (ongoing support and maintenance), and retirement (end-of-life activities); conceptualization and inception together roughly refer to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering.

E2553.name: sprint
E2553.text: sprint; also called: iteration, agile sprint, development cycle. The agile development process flow consists of conceptualization, inception (creation of the team and arranging funds and resources), iteration or sprint (the development cycle, which includes all the other stages of the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC)), release (testing, training, and documentation, and deployment), production (ongoing support and maintenance), and retirement (end-of-life activities); conceptualization and inception together roughly refer to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering. An agile iteration or sprint typically requires four to six weeks, whereas the whole Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) may take six to nine months, because the sprint does not try to do everything. An agile sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery: requirements are based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, then testing including training and documentation, then delivery to production. To deliver within an agile sprint, the development team holds daily meetings or brainstorming, provides a live demonstration after each iteration, and regularly collects quick feedback from stakeholders and customers, which is shared with the team before the next sprint so that it can be addressed; this keeps the team agile by making changes based on feedback as quickly as possible.

E2570.name: optimization
E2570.text: optimization. Optimization in virtual reality (VR) can be considered from two perspectives: optimized experience, that is, psychophysiological experience optimization, and optimized resource utilization or resource requirement, that is, technological optimization; these requirements are present in any extended reality (XR) system, but they gain more prominence in an immersive experience. In virtual reality (VR), experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction. In virtual reality (VR), effective resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience, without compromising it and, to the extent possible, without reducing its quality; this requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience. Compared with a high-end graphics workstation, the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage, so the Oculus Quest 2 application required optimization to reduce its size and associated computations, including memory access, because reducing the size reduces rendering requirements and the associated memory access. The Oculus Quest 2 application used a cloud computing-based optimization in which all videos, not images, were stored in the cloud because videos take up more space; when a user selected a video thumbnail from the Oculus Quest 2 video player, the video was loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally, reducing storage and data-access requirements.

Extended reality (XR) systems, and virtual reality (VR) systems in particular, are generally resource-hungry; if their resource requirements are too high, the systems will not be affordable and it will be difficult to make products for the masses, where affordability is a major concern. In virtual reality (VR), effective resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience, without compromising it and, to the extent possible, without reducing its quality; this requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience. The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience. The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) in Unity has many pipeline stages optimized by the pipeline implementation itself, and it takes care of pipeline-implementation optimization to some extent, so a developer need not manage those aspects and resource requirements are minimized.

E2574.text: susceptibility to motion sickness. E2578.name: cybersickness mitigation strategies
E2578.text: cybersickness mitigation strategies. Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience. The challenge in developing cybersickness mitigation strategies is to avoid compromising presence, which is indirectly related to user experience.

E2586.name: user-controlled virtual reality tour
E2586.text: user-controlled virtual reality tour. Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

E2587.name: system-controlled virtual reality tour
E2587.text: system-controlled virtual reality tour. Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements. System-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to concentrate more on the experience itself. Lack of user involvement in system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement.

E2588.name: system-controlled tour
E2588.text: system-controlled tour; also called: system-automated tour. In a virtual reality (VR) tour, a system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system forces the user to move from one place to another. A realistic walking experience in a system-controlled tour is important because it helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of the difference between realistic and unrealistic elements. System-controlled tours, also described as system-automated tours, typically do not allow continuous user input, making it difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural. When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow. A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold. Once a C# script is attached as a component to a game object in Unity as part of the design or development, it starts working whenever the game is executed, and it allows the developer to trigger game events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input in any way the developer wants.

E2593.name: optic flow
E2593.text: optic flow; also called: scene-change speed, visual speed. Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene. When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow. A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed. The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

E2606.text: speed estimation model. The empirical study was conducted to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another and to propose a speed estimation model.

E2607.name: walking behavior
E2607.text: walking behavior. In the empirical study, participant heights were recorded because earlier studies indicate that height affects walking behavior, and the participants' heights ranged from 150 to 184 centimeters.

E2608.name: corridor experiment
E2608.text: corridor experiment. The corridor experiment used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances of 20, 20, 13, 16, 6.4, 19, and 4 meters from the start.

E2609.name: video recording
E2609.text: video recording. Video recordings of the user's footsteps were made with a Samsung M30 smartphone camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs; the recording started just before the user started walking and was captured at 30 frames per second.

E2610.name: data-analysis stage
E2610.text: data-analysis stage. In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

E2611.name: step frequency
E2611.text: step frequency; also called: instantaneous step frequency. In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps. When step frequency was plotted against distance, a pattern more or less followed by all participants was seen: step frequency started low, increased to a maximum, plateaued, and then decreased to zero at the target painting where the user stopped to click a photo; this pattern is called the slow-in-slow-out pattern.

E2616.name: slow-in-slow-out walking pattern
E2616.text: slow-in-slow-out walking pattern. The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero. The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids, and the weights of those sinusoids are calculated from empirical data.

E2617.name: fourier series
E2617.text: fourier series; also called: fourier-series approximation, fourier-series expansion, fourier expansion. The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero. A Fourier series with appropriate weights can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, and a practical approximation can be obtained by taking the first few terms of the corresponding Fourier expansion. The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids, and the weights of those sinusoids are calculated from empirical data. The instantaneous step frequency f(x) is computed from the Fourier-series expression f(x) = (4/π) × 1.8 × Σ_{k=0}^{d/2−1} [1/(2k+1) × sin((2k+1)ωx)], where ω = 2πf0, f0 is the initial frequency and equals 1/(2d), and d is the distance between the source and destination.

E2621.name: virtual walking
E2621.text: virtual walking. In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

E2622.name: actual movement speed
E2622.text: actual movement speed; also called: actual walking velocity, actual instantaneous walking speed, actual walking speed. In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement. A virtual tour should not change the scene at the user's actual walking velocity; instead it should make the perceived scene-change speed differ from the actual movement speed so that the user perceives natural walking behavior. The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency. In the model, the actual walking speed V_actual is calculated as V_actual = f(x) × 0.157 × (h × 1.72)^2, where f(x) is the instantaneous step frequency as a function of distance x and h is the user's height.

E2627.name: natural walking speed model
E2627.text: natural walking speed model; also called: instantaneous speed, instantaneous natural walking speed, instantaneous natural walking speed model, natural walking-speed model, natural walking model. The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking. The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed. The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture. Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection. The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables.

E2630.text: constant speed; also called: constant average speed, constant. The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed. The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture. Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection. The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables. Box plots of the realism and preference ratings showed that instantaneous speed produced higher realism ratings and higher user preference than constant speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed these differences were statistically significant.

E2637.name: natural walking model
E2637.text: natural walking model. The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement. The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world. The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

E2642.name: virtual reality environment
E2642.text: virtual reality environment. In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

E2643.name: virtual reality exposure duration
names: duration of exposure to a virtual world
E2643.text: virtual reality exposure duration; also called: duration of VR exposure, duration of exposure to a virtual world, overall exposure duration, exposure time. The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects. A larger virtual reality (VR) environment leads to a longer duration of VR exposure because the user needs to cover a larger geographical area. Increasing the virtual travel or navigation speed reduces the duration of exposure to a virtual world because a higher speed lowers the time needed to travel and explore the entire geographical area. Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required. Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

Increasing the virtual travel or navigation speed reduces the duration of exposure to a virtual world because a higher speed lowers the time needed to travel and explore the entire geographical area. To provide a realistic walking experience in a virtual world, virtual travel speed cannot be modified arbitrarily; an arbitrary speed imposed on the user while navigating may not be a good idea.

E2646.name: travel time
E2646.text: travel time; also called: travelling time, time to travel, total travel time, travel times, traveling time, travel duration, t. Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

E2647.name: interaction time
E2647.text: interaction time. The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects. In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored. In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI. In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, the duration of exposure can be optimized, under a limit on interaction time, by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time required to experience all points of interest (POIs) or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit for navigation and interaction.

E2651.name: semi-interactive tour
E2651.text: semi-interactive tour. A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

E2653.name: semi-interactive virtual tour
E2653.text: semi-interactive virtual tour; also called: virtual tour, virtual reality tour, VR tour, semi-interactive virtual reality tour. In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI. In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, the duration of exposure can be optimized, under a limit on interaction time, by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time required to experience all points of interest (POIs) or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit for navigation and interaction. Optimizing the duration of exposure in a virtual reality (VR) tour is expected to optimize the prevalence and onset of cyber sickness, because exposure duration and cyber sickness are directly related.

E2655.name: weighted graph
E2655.text: weighted graph; also called: graph. The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world. The graph G used to represent the virtual world need not be complete, because in a realistic environment there may not always be a direct path from one place to another. In the mapping of the virtual world to the graph, each point of interest (POI) is a node, while a single object or structure is not necessarily a single node because it may contain multiple points of interest. The optimum travel path problem covering all points of interest (POIs) is to find a path P in the given graph G that covers all vertices in V, which are the POIs, and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout, so that the user gets a realistic feeling.

For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices. In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act). After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

E2672.name: graph
E2672.text: graph; also called: graph representation. The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G. The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G. After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances. The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph. Because the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver's optimal path p_opt may contain hypothetical edges that are not in the original graph G, the algorithm post-processes p_opt into p_dash_opt by checking each path edge and replacing each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G with the shortest path between those endpoints in G.

E2673.name: total travel time

In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

E2674.name: travel-time minimisation problem

The graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is not assumed to be a complete graph, so there may be no Hamiltonian path in that graph, where a Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once. For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path. E2731.name: Majuli
E2731.text: Majuli. Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam, surrounded on all sides by the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries. Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total. Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest. Majuli is the world's largest inhabited river island, located in eastern India on the river Brahmaputra and surrounded by the Brahmaputra and its tributary.

E2732.name: Auniati Satra
E2732.text: Auniati Satra. Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest. Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking may take up to a day, including stoppage at the points of interest, and a full-day exposure to a virtual reality (VR) tour is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness. The system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour of Auniati Satra uses walking-based exploration with the natural walking speed model to provide a realistic experience. E2740.name: resource
E2740.text: resource. Extended reality (XR), in particular virtual reality (VR), is resource hungry, meaning that XR and VR require a lot of resources. The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience. In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers. Each resource type in extended reality (XR) can be optimized separately, but such optimization is not easy because the considerations vary widely and include money such as availability of funds and how resources are managed, availability of the resources before use, policy issues, and geopolitical issues. Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

E2757.name: interface object
E2757.text: interface object. The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

E2759.name: binary representation
E2759.text: binary representation. Computers understand only binary representation, that is zeros and ones, whereas humans perceive realistic representation, not strings of zeros and ones.

E2760.name: representation
E2760.text: representation. Computers understand only binary representation, that is zeros and ones, whereas humans perceive realistic representation, not strings of zeros and ones. The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it. The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

E2761.name: synthesis
E2761.text: synthesis. The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

E2762.name: generic graphics system
E2762.text: generic graphics system. A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller. In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data. The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.

E2763.name: host computer
E2763.text: host computer. A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller. In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

E2764.name: display controller
E2764.text: display controller; also called: graphics card. A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller. In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data. The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen. The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU. The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage.

E2765.name: video memory
E2765.text: video memory; also called: video random-access memory, VRAM. A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller. The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage. Video memory is the dedicated part of the overall memory hierarchy of the computer where the digital image is stored, typically as part of a separate graphics unit, and in modern graphics cards it is sometimes called video random-access memory (VRAM). The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

E2766.name: video controller
E2766.text: video controller. A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller. The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

E2767.name: display command
E2767.text: display command; also called: display commands. In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

E2768.name: interaction data
E2768.text: interaction data. In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

E2769.name: image generation
E2769.text: image generation; also called: rendering. The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen. Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component. The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU. The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

E2770.name: analog voltage
E2770.text: analog voltage; also called: analog voltages. The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

E2771.name: graphic device
E2771.text: graphic device. Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

E2772.name: vector scan device
E2772.text: vector scan device; also called: random scan, stroke writing, calligraphic devices. Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices. Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived. Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required.

E2773.name: geometric primitive
E2773.text: geometric primitive; also called: primitives. Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

E2774.name: line
E2774.text: line. Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived. Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels. In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations. Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.

E2775.name: curve
E2775.text: curve. Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived. Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation. In polynomial representation of a curve, a more complex curve is represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming. In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece. Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

E2776.name: precision
E2776.text: precision. Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required. Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.

E2777.name: raster scan device
E2777.text: raster scan device; also called: raster scan displays. Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices. A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning. Commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and any device with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

E2778.name: pixel grid
E2778.text: pixel grid. A display device uses a pixel grid to render an image, and points on that pixel grid can only have integer coordinates. Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

E2779.name: scanning
E2779.text: scanning; also called: raster scanning. A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning.

E2780.name: raster scan rendering
E2780.text: raster scan rendering. In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.

E2781.name: vector scan rendering
E2781.text: vector scan rendering. Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.

E2782.name: television
E2782.text: television. Commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and any device with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

E2783.name: raster scan system
E2783.text: raster scan system; also called: raster scan device. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s. The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device. In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing. Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

E2784.name: frame buffer
E2784.text: frame buffer. The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.

E2785.name: memory location
E2785.text: memory location. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

E2786.name: bit string
E2786.text: bit string. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

E2787.name: screen resolution
E2787.text: screen resolution. The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.

E2788.name: light-emitting element
E2788.text: light-emitting element; also called: pixel element. In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing. In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities. Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.

E2789.name: screen refreshing
E2789.text: screen refreshing. Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

E2790.name: refresh rate
E2790.text: refresh rate. The refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on a screen, is represented in hertz, and a good refresh rate for most devices is 60 hertz. A higher refresh rate is always preferable for a virtual reality (VR) experience because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer usage, where the screen and the eyes are at a reasonable distance.

E2791.name: virtual reality screen
E2791.text: virtual reality screen; also called: VR screen. A higher refresh rate is always preferable for a virtual reality (VR) experience because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer usage, where the screen and the eyes are at a reasonable distance.

E2792.name: color display
E2792.text: color display. In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities. Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.
