E2796.name: primary color
E2796.text: primary color. In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb). In a colored light source model, the red, green, and blue components of the source intensity are computed individually, and their combination gives the perception of any color.

E2797.name: three-dimensional computer graphics pipeline
E2797.text: three-dimensional computer graphics pipeline; also called: 3D computer graphics pipeline, 3D graphics pipeline. The three-dimensional (3D) computer graphics pipeline (3D graphics pipeline) is a stage-wise process of computation starting from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.

E2798.name: object representation
E2798.text: object representation. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion. The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

E2799.name: color value
E2799.text: color value. The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages. The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

E2802.name: display mechanism
E2802.text: display mechanism. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

E2803.name: local coordinate system
E2803.text: local coordinate system. The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. E2804.name: modeling transformation
E2804.text: modeling transformation; also called: geometric transformation, stage 2. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion. The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description. Modeling transformation, also called geometric transformation and referred to as stage 2, applies operations to an object's local or object coordinate system description to place the object in a common scene or world coordinate system so that multiple objects can be assembled into a scene. The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

E2805.name: world coordinate system
E2805.text: world coordinate system; also called: world coordinate reference frame. The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible. Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system. The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.

E2806.name: device coordinate system

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer. E2809.name: hidden surface removal
E2809.text: hidden surface removal. Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation. In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal. In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

E2810.name: projection transformation

E2811.name: window-to-viewport transformation
E2811.text: window-to-viewport transformation. The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy). In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

E2816.name: three-dimensional object representation
E2816.text: three-dimensional object representation; also called: 3D object representation. The fundamental objective of three-dimensional (3D) object representation is to balance the requirement to represent objects of different shapes and sizes with their intricate details so that they render realistically in a synthesized environment, rather than as simplistic geometric approximations that lose realism, and the requirement to make the operations of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline efficient in space and time. In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, the computation of pixel intensities depends on the object representation, and more complex representations lead to more complex calculations, so realistic rendering can suffer lags or require expensive hardware if the computation is not efficient.

E2817.name: pixel intensity
E2817.text: pixel intensity; also called: pixel intensities. In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display. A table stores the calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, and a lighting-model pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so that the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.

E2818.name: three-dimensional object representation technique
E2818.text: three-dimensional object representation technique; also called: 3D object representation technique. A single three-dimensional (3D) object representation technique is not sufficient because different object representation techniques are available, and the appropriate technique must be chosen for a particular problem. The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

E2819.name: point sample rendering
E2819.text: point sample rendering. The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation. Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes. In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques. In point sample rendering, the captured points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved. Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

E2822.name: mesh representation
E2822.text: mesh representation. Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used. In mesh representation, a greater number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces but makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained. Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.

Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used. The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience. Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input. Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles. In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.

E2841.name: spline representation
E2841.text: spline representation. Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation. Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations. In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece. In spline representation, the polynomial pieces that make up the complete curve must join smoothly, and certain geometric and other properties need to be satisfied by each piece.

E2852.name: space partitioning representation
E2852.text: space partitioning representation. Space partitioning representation is a broad category of object representation in which the three-dimensional (3D) space occupied by an object is divided into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so that any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object can be represented by representing the occupied regions. A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation. Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods. Specialized sophisticated representation techniques are often required for application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects rather than the broader boundary or space partitioning categories.

E2858.text: skeletal model. E2860.name: pipeline stage
E2860.text: pipeline stage; also called: pipeline stages, stages. In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur. Render pipeline support is an important graphics support offered by Unity, providing support to implement the entire render pipeline—camera and view transform, lighting, meshes, materials, textures, shaders, and environment creation (world scene or world-coordinate-system scene creation, special environments such as skies, and different visual effects)—and also letting the user have customized control over individual pipeline stages. The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) in Unity has many pipeline stages optimized by the pipeline implementation itself, and it takes care of pipeline-implementation optimization to some extent, so a developer need not manage those aspects and resource requirements are minimized.

E2863.name: screen coordinate
E2863.text: screen coordinate; also called: screen coordinates, device coordinates. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description. The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

E2864.name: object coordinate system
E2864.text: object coordinate system; also called: coordinate reference frame. Modeling transformation, also called geometric transformation and referred to as stage 2, applies operations to an object's local or object coordinate system description to place the object in a common scene or world coordinate system so that multiple objects can be assembled into a scene. An object's local or object coordinate system description is an individual definition of the object in which its position and dimension are defined in its own coordinate reference frame.

E2865.name: dimension

E2866.name: translation
E2866.text: translation. A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing. In the worked example, transforming rectangle ABCD from its local coordinate system to the chimney-like shape A′, B′, C′, D′ in the world coordinate scene cannot be done with one basic transformation and requires two basic transformations, scaling and translation. In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5). In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

E2867.name: angle
E2867.text: angle. The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

E2893.name: computer graphics pipeline
E2893.text: computer graphics pipeline; also called: CG pipeline. The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline.

E2894.name: color computation
E2894.text: color computation. In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception.

E2895.name: shading model
E2895.text: shading model. In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception. In computer graphics, lighting models and shading models are distinct, although they may physically represent more or less similar things, and they are differentiated by the computation involved: lighting models involve more computation than shading models, and shading models are used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience. Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, and they rely on lighting models.

E2896.name: depth
E2896.text: depth; also called: depth information. In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

E2897.name: continuous intensity value
E2897.text: continuous intensity value. Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values.

E2898.name: discrete value
E2898.text: discrete value. Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values.

E2899.name: surface point
E2899.text: surface point. A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived. In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point. In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec). In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed. The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

E2900.name: reflected light
E2900.text: reflected light. A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived. In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point.

E2901.name: simple lighting model
E2901.text: simple lighting model. In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec). In the simple lighting model, the ambient light component is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces. In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface. In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot. The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

E2902.name: ambient light intensity
E2902.text: ambient light intensity; also called: I amb. In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec). The ambient component of the reflected light intensity is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light Ka.

E2906.name: ambient light component
E2906.text: ambient light component. In the simple lighting model, the ambient light component is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

E2907.name: diffuse light component
E2907.text: diffuse light component. In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface.

E2908.name: specular reflection component
E2908.text: specular reflection component. In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

E2909.name: reflected light intensity
E2909.text: reflected light intensity; also called: intensity of light reflected. The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity. The ambient component of the reflected light intensity is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light Ka.

E2910.name: incident light intensity
E2910.text: incident light intensity. The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.

E2911.name: reflection coefficient
E2911.text: reflection coefficient; also called: reflectivity, k, kd, ks. The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity. The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light. Each of the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model has a value from 0.0 to 1.0, where a value close to 0 represents a dull surface with no reflection because most of the light is absorbed, a value close to 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface where all light gets reflected, and varying the coefficients generates different effects between dull and shiny surfaces.

E2912.name: diffuse reflection
E2912.text: diffuse reflection. The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light. The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

E2916.name: specular reflection coefficient
E2916.text: specular reflection coefficient; also called: Ks. The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light. The specular component is computed as the specular reflection coefficient for direct light Ks times the source light intensity Is times the dot product of the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, raised to the power Ns, and it is 0 when V dot r is not greater than 0.

E2920.name: dot product
E2920.text: dot product; also called: vector dot products. The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection. The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r. The specular component is computed as the specular reflection coefficient for direct light Ks times the source light intensity Is times the dot product of the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, raised to the power Ns, and it is 0 when V dot r is not greater than 0. The ideal specular reflection direction vector r is represented by r equal to twice the dot product of the light source direction vector L and the surface normal vector N, multiplied by the surface normal vector N, minus the light source direction vector L. The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

E2928.name: light intensity
E2928.text: light intensity; also called: intensity of light. In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed. The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect. Unity provides support for realistic lighting on game objects, allowing developers to specify the intensity, direction, and color of the light and to render real-time shadows using shadow mapping.

E2929.name: radial intensity attenuation factor

The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect. In the simple lighting model modified for radial and angular intensity attenuation, the I_M intensity component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse reflection component I_D and the specular reflection component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors; if those factors are 1, the model reduces to I_M + I_D + I_SPEC.

E2939.name: colored light source model
E2939.text: colored light source model. E2947.name: intensity mapping
E2947.text: intensity mapping. In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display. A table stores the calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, and a lighting-model pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so that the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.

E2961.name: two-dimensional display
E2961.text: two-dimensional display; also called: 2D display. The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

E2962.name: view coordinate system
E2962.text: view coordinate system; also called: 3D view coordinate system, 2D view coordinate system. The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters. The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point. The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N. Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

E2963.name: three-dimensional world coordinate system
E2963.text: three-dimensional world coordinate system; also called: 3D world coordinate system. The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

E2964.name: two-dimensional view plane
E2964.text: two-dimensional view plane; also called: 2D view plane. E2965.name: two-dimensional device coordinate space
E2965.text: two-dimensional device coordinate space; also called: 2D device coordinate space. E2966.name: three-dimensional viewing transformation
E2966.text: three-dimensional viewing transformation; also called: 3D viewing transformation, 3D transformation. The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters. Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

E2967.name: world coordinates
E2967.text: world coordinates; also called: 3D world coordinate description. Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components. The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience. The Unity editor supports scene creation by transferring objects from local coordinates to world coordinates and by providing tools to create and modify environmental features such as landforms, vegetation, and the landscape.

E2970.name: camera parameters
E2970.text: camera parameters. The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

E2971.name: origin vector
E2971.text: origin vector; also called: camera origin vector. The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point. The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

E2981.name: view volume
E2981.text: view volume. A view volume is a three-dimensional (3D) region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is projected onto the view plane, so objects inside the view volume are projected and objects outside it are discarded. Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection. For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected. The naive clipping method computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, and this calculation is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums. A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

E2982.name: perspective projection
E2982.text: perspective projection. Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated. For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected. A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations. For perspective projection, a canonical view volume is obtained by converting the frustum into a normalized unit cube, which requires scaling and shearing operations to change its size and shape and involves more computation than the parallel case. A perspective projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a perspective projection matrix that is more complex than the parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, which is typically assumed to be at the origin but not always; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

E2983.name: center of projection
E2983.text: center of projection; also called: point of projection. Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated. Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet. A perspective projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a perspective projection matrix that is more complex than the parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, which is typically assumed to be at the origin but not always; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

E2984.name: parallel projection
E2984.text: parallel projection. Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet. For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected. A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations. For parallel projection, a canonical view volume is obtained by scaling an arbitrarily defined view volume into a unit cube. A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

E2996.name: viewport
E2996.text: viewport; also called: 2D viewport. A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy). In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

E2997.name: device space
E2997.text: device space; also called: device-space. A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions. In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles. In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.

E2998.name: window point
E2998.text: window point. The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy). To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

E3003.name: computational complexity
E3003.text: computational complexity. Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced. Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation. In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold.

E3005.name: occlusion
E3005.text: occlusion; also called: occluded. E3006.name: geometric transformation
E3006.text: geometric transformation; also called: modeling. The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

E3007.name: view pipeline
E3007.text: view pipeline. In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

E3008.name: continuous coordinate system
E3008.text: continuous coordinate system. The device coordinate system used to define the two-dimensional (2D) viewport is a continuous coordinate system, so its coordinate values can be any real number.

E3009.name: mapping algorithm
E3009.text: mapping algorithm. Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

E3017.name: circle
E3017.text: circle. In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles. Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.

E3018.name: line rendering
E3018.text: line rendering; also called: line-rendering, line-rendering method. A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication. Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines. Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.

E3019.name: floating-point operation
E3019.text: floating-point operation. A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication. The basic idea for rendering a shape on a screen is to map the original shape to the set of pixels that represent it as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations. For lines, floating-point operations can be completely eliminated, whereas for other shapes they may not be completely eliminated but can be minimized.

E3021.name: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm
E3021.text: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm; also called: Bresenham line-drawing algorithm. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations. The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment. In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

E3036.name: distortion
E3036.text: distortion. Aliasing is distortion that may occur in an original shape after scan conversion because scan conversion renders pixels that are close to points on the original shape rather than exactly rendering the points, so an approximated line may not exactly match the original line. If aliasing is left unaddressed, it may lead to distortion that is visible with a change in resolution and that will reduce the quality of experience. Anti-aliasing operations are additional operations, using complex algorithms, that remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing so that the end effect is better. The challenge in virtual reality (VR) rendering is to handle a computationally complex rendering process without the user perceiving lag or distortion.

E3041.name: graphics library
E3041.text: graphics library; also called: library, graphics libraries. A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements. Examples of graphics libraries include OpenGL, which stands for Open Graphics Library, Vulkan, and Direct3D. The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks. The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application. Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.

E3044.name: layered virtual reality software architecture
E3044.text: layered virtual reality software architecture. A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

Unity's scripting environment is set up automatically when the Unity package is installed, Unity supports integrated development environments (IDEs) such as Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and JetBrains Rider, and on Windows and Mac the default Unity installation also installs Visual Studio, which can be used to develop and compile scripts. Unlike most other assets, C# scripts in Unity are usually created directly within Unity, using the interface provided by the integrated development environment (IDE), by choosing Assets, then Create, then C# Script from the main menu, and the new script is created in the folder selected in the project panel when the project is started. Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems are primarily programming tasks, with the amount of programming depending on the required functionality: a basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment (IDE) support, whereas a customized experience requires scripting, which involves more programming.

The Unity editor interface includes the scene view, game view, hierarchy window, inspector window, toolbar, status bar, project window, and console window. E3225.name: Unity physics engine
E3225.text: Unity physics engine; also called: Unity's physics engine. Unity's physics engine simulates physical laws in a project so that objects correctly accelerate and respond to collisions. The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling. The isKinematic property, used with a Unity rigid body, can remove the object from physics engine control and allow it to be moved kinematically from a script, so it does not automatically follow gravity, and the developer can choose whether the object follows gravity.

E3226.name: rigid body
E3226.text: rigid body; also called: rigid bodies, rigid body component. The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling. A rigid body in Unity is a concept and a property that, when attached to a game object, allows the game object to respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing from a surface appears realistic in accordance with everyday experience. The isKinematic property, used with a Unity rigid body, can remove the object from physics engine control and allow it to be moved kinematically from a script, so it does not automatically follow gravity, and the developer can choose whether the object follows gravity. In Unity, static colliders can be added to a game object without a rigid body component to create floors, walls, and other motionless elements of a scene. In Unity, a joint connects a rigid body to another rigid body or to a fixed point in space, can apply forces that move the rigid bodies, has limits that restrict that movement, and can be used to model the realistic movement of specific objects or characters such as a ball and socket joint like a hip or shoulder, any skeletal joint, doors, finger joints, or a piece of elastic.

E3227.name: collider
E3227.text: collider; also called: colliders. The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling. A collider in Unity defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions, allows the developer to deal with the object's shape after it collides with another object, and includes types that are primitive colliders such as box collider, sphere collider, and capsule collider, or mesh collider, which is more processor-intensive but accurate. In Unity, static colliders can be added to a game object without a rigid body component to create floors, walls, and other motionless elements of a scene. A collider in Unity configured as a trigger using the isTrigger property does not behave as a solid object and simply allows other colliders to pass through.

E3228.name: physics articulation
E3228.text: physics articulation; also called: articulation, articulations. The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling. Physics articulation (articulation) in Unity is the overall movement of a structure or object comprising joints, and it provides realistic physics behavior that involves joints. In Unity, articulations can be configured via the articulation body class or the corresponding articulation body component, which provides inbuilt support that automatically implements joint constraints, so a developer does not need to control each individual joint to make a complex figure move realistically. The articulation body class in Unity represents articulation bodies as a logical tree in which each node is a joint and each parent-child relationship reflects mutually constrained relative motion, so the relations and relative movements of the joints define the overall articulation.

E3261.name: development environment
E3261.text: development environment; also called: Unity development environment, built-in environment. In the Unity development environment, built-in support gives a good-quality experience that is only what the system provides, so to obtain a more customized experience according to the programmer's expectations and needs, the programmer must write scripts or small pieces of code to change the built-in support. In the Unity development environment, installing a software development kit (SDK) extends the built-in environment, as shown by Vuforia adding image-recognition functionality and device-specific SDKs being used to access device-specific sensory or input data.

E3262.name: scripting environment
E3262.text: scripting environment. Unity's scripting environment is set up automatically when the Unity package is installed, Unity supports integrated development environments (IDEs) such as Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and JetBrains Rider, and on Windows and Mac the default Unity installation also installs Visual Studio, which can be used to develop and compile scripts. In Unity's scripting environment, the Destroy function, which comes under the MonoBehaviour class, destroys a game object from the scene after a specified delay, typically in seconds; for example, Destroy(gameObject, 5f) makes the game object no longer visible in the scene five seconds after the function is called. The scripting environment supports standard conditional if-else statements. Loops in the scripting environment can be entry-controlled or exit-controlled: for and while loops are entry-controlled because the loop condition is checked before the loop body executes, and a do-while loop is exit-controlled because the loop body executes at least once and the condition is checked after the loop body executes.

E3263.name: package
E3263.text: package; also called: packages, Unity package, external packages. Unity's scripting environment is set up automatically when the Unity package is installed, Unity supports integrated development environments (IDEs) such as Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and JetBrains Rider, and on Windows and Mac the default Unity installation also installs Visual Studio, which can be used to develop and compile scripts. If a system is to be deployed on a specified hardware platform, head-mounted display (HMD), or smart glasses, and that platform provides features or functions not included in the built-in support provided by the Unity environment, the developer imports software development kits (SDKs) or packages to access and use those platform-specific functions. In the Unity layered architecture, the application is the top layer, and the software development kit (SDK) layer, which is positioned on top of the Unity layer, is treated as part of the installed Unity package whose application programming interfaces (APIs) are used. Unity's built-in support for object recognition or computer vision operations, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking, is not extensive and not very good, so seamless and efficient performance of these operations requires external packages. The basic steps for integrating a software development kit (SDK) into the Unity development environment are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK package into the Unity environment, use the functions of both Unity and the SDK, and then compile, build, and deploy.

E3297.text: event function. An event function in Unity is a function that Unity activates in response to an event that occurs during gameplay, and when the event happens, Unity passes control to the event function, its body executes, and then control is passed back to Unity. Common Unity gameplay events and their event functions include regular update events, such as the Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate functions; initialization events, such as the Start and Awake functions; graphical user interface (GUI) events, such as the OnGUI, OnMouseOver, and OnMouseDown functions; physics events, such as the OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit functions, which relate to contact being made or broken; and other physics-related events, such as the OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit functions, which are called when a collider is configured as a trigger. Unity's event functions can be used to impose realistic behavior, such as physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in graphical user interface (GUI) event functions.

E3339.name: coroutine
E3339.text: coroutine. A coroutine in Unity is a method that allows a developer to spread tasks across several frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off on the following frame. Coroutines are not threads and are not designed to behave like threads; synchronous operations within a coroutine still execute on the main thread, and coroutine execution does not spawn individual threads. A gradual opacity fade of an object is visible only when its alpha or opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so that Unity renders the intermediate values; a fade function called only once is not perceivable, so the fade must be defined as a coroutine and started so that the change is spread frame by frame.

E3349.name: build
E3349.text: build; also called: Build and Run. In the Unity development environment, after the script is written and the system is built, the last stage is to publish or deploy the system, and the editor's Build Settings window, reached by going to File Build Settings, contains all settings and options to publish the build. In the Unity development environment's editor, the Build Settings window's Scenes in Build panel manages which scenes are included in the build, its platform section selects the platform to which the system is deployed, and the Build or Build and Run button begins the build process. The basic steps for integrating a software development kit (SDK) into the Unity development environment are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK package into the Unity environment, use the functions of both Unity and the SDK, and then compile, build, and deploy. For the Android platform, the build is created by following File > Build Settings > Android > Switch Platform, connecting the Android device through a universal serial bus (USB) cable with USB debugging enabled, and selecting Build and Run, which creates an Android package (APK) file and deploys it directly to the device; alternatively, the Android package (APK) file can be developed first and then transferred and installed separately.

E3359.name: object detection
E3359.text: object detection. Vuforia is an augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking. Unity's built-in support for object recognition or computer vision operations, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking, is not extensive and not very good, so seamless and efficient performance of these operations requires external packages.

The Vuforia configuration requires a Vuforia account and license, and the license is added to the Unity project from that Vuforia account.

E3363.name: vuforia engine
E3363.text: vuforia engine. To install Vuforia in Unity, a new Unity project is created using the universal 3D template or an empty project, and the Vuforia engine is added to the project assets either by downloading the Vuforia SDK for Unity from developer.vuforia.com or by manually importing the package as a custom package, after which it can be used directly in the Unity editor. Vuforia setup requires creating a new database on the Vuforia website, adding the images or markers to be tracked to that database so the Vuforia engine can recognize them, and downloading the database package file and importing it into the project as a custom package because the database is required for recognition. An image target behavior script is attached to or used to modify the behavior of a Vuforia image target, and it performs the operations after the Vuforia engine recognizes the marker. In the sample marker-based augmented reality (AR) application, the Earth image is the marker, and when a device running the Android package (APK) file captures a matching colored image on a mobile screen, desk, or paper, the Vuforia engine recognizes the marker and displays a three-dimensional (3D) model in place of the marker; the displayed image must match the original image in color, shape, and size.
